snippet: A system of linear equations has no solution, or exactly one solution, or infinitely many solutions.
body_xml:
<note type="theorem" source_type="theorem_key">
    <paragraph>A system of linear equations has</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>no solution, or</item>
      <item>exactly one solution, or</item>
      <item>infinitely many solutions.</item>
    </list>
  </note>

title: Example 1
snippet: Example 1: Example 1 Solve system (3). Solution The elimination procedure is shown here with and without matrix notation, and the results are placed side by side for comparison: x_{1} & - & 2 x_{2} & + & x_{3} & = & 0 & & 2 x_{2} & - & 8...
body_xml: Example 1 Solve system (3). Solution The elimination procedure is shown here with and without matrix notation, and the results are placed side by side for comparison: $$x_{1} & - & 2 x_{2} & + & x_{3} & = & 0 & & 2 x_{2} & - & 8 x_{3} & = & 8 5 x_{1} & & & - & 5 x_{3} & = & 10 \begin{bmatrix} 1 & - 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & - 8 & 8 \\ 5 & 0 & - 5 & 10 \end{bmatrix}$$ Keep $$x_{1}$$ in the first equation and eliminate it from the other equations. To do so, add $$- 5$$ times equation 1 to equation 3. After some practice, this type of calculation is usually performed mentally: The result of this calculation is written in place of the original third equation: $$x_{1} & - & 2 x_{2} & + & x_{3} & = & 0 & & 2 x_{2} & - & 8 x_{3} & = & 8 & & 10 x_{2} & - & 10 x_{3} & = & 10 \begin{bmatrix} 1 & - 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & - 8 & 8 \\ 0 & 10 & - 10 & 10 \end{bmatrix}$$ Now, multiply equation 2 by $$\frac{1}{2}$$ in order to obtain $$1$$ as the coefficient for $$x_{2}$$ . (This calculation will simplify the arithmetic in the next step.) $$x_{1} & - & 2 x_{2} & + & x_{3} & = & 0 & & x_{2} & - & 4 x_{3} & = & 4 & & 10 x_{2} & - & 10 x_{3} & = & 10 \begin{bmatrix} 1 & - 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & - 4 & 4 \\ 0 & 10 & - 10 & 10 \end{bmatrix}$$ Use the $$x_{2}$$ in equation 2 to eliminate the $$10x_{2}$$ in equation 3. The “mental’’ computation is The result of this calculation is written in place of the previous third equation (row): $$x_{1} & - & 2 x_{2} & + & x_{3} & = & 0 & & x_{2} & - & 4 x_{3} & = & 4 & & & & 30 x_{3} & = & - 30 \begin{bmatrix} 1 & - 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & - 4 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 30 & - 30 \end{bmatrix}$$ Now, multiply equation 3 by $$\frac{1}{30}$$ in order to obtain $$1$$ as the coefficient for $$x_{3}$$ . (This calculation will simplify the arithmetic in the next step.) $$x_{1} & - & 2 x_{2} & + & x_{3} & = & 0 & & x_{2} & - & 4 x_{3} & = & 4 & & & & x_{3} & = & - 1 \begin{bmatrix} 1 & - 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & - 4 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & - 1 \end{bmatrix}$$ The new system has a triangular form (the intuitive term triangular will be replaced by a precise term in the next section): $$x_{1} & - & 2 x_{2} & + & x_{3} & = & 0 & & x_{2} & - & 4 x_{3} & = & 4 & & & & x_{3} & = & - 1 \begin{bmatrix} 1 & - 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & - 4 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & - 1 \end{bmatrix}$$ Eventually, you want to eliminate the $$- 2x_{2}$$ term from equation 1, but it is more efficient to use the $$x_{3}$$ in equation 3 first, to eliminate the $$- 4x_{3}$$ and $$+ x_{3}$$ terms in equations 2 and 1. The two “mental” calculations are It is convenient to combine the results of these two operations: $$x_{1} - 2 x_{2} & & = & 1 & & x_{2} & & = & 0 & & & x_{3} & = & - 1 & & \left[\right. 1 & - 2 & 0 & 1 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 0 & 0 & 1 & - 1 \left]\right.$$ Now, having cleaned out the column above the $$x_{3}$$ in equation 3, move back to the $$x_{2}$$ in equation 2 and use it to eliminate the $$- 2x_{2}$$ above it. Because of the previous work with $$x_{3}$$ , there is now no arithmetic involving $$x_{3}$$ terms. Add $$2$$ times equation 2 to equation 1 and obtain the system: $$x_{1} & & & = & 1 & & x_{2} & & = & 0 & & & x_{3} & = & - 1 & \left[\right. 1 & 0 & 0 & 1 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 0 & 0 & 1 & - 1 \left]\right.$$ Each of the original equations determines a plane in three-dimensional space. The point $$(1 \text{,} 0 \text{,−} 1)$$ lies in all three planes. The work is essentially done. It shows that the only solution of the original system is $$(1 \text{,} 0 \text{,−} 1)$$ . However, since there are so many calculations involved, it is a good practice to check the work. To verify that $$( 1 , 0 ,- 1 )$$ is a solution, substitute these values into the left side of the original system, and compute: $$1 \left(\right. 1 \left.\right) & - & 2 \left(\right. 0 \left.\right) & + & 1 \left(\right. - 1 \left.\right) & = & 1 & - & 0 & - & 1 & = & 0 & & 2 \left(\right. 0 \left.\right) & - & 8 \left(\right. - 1 \left.\right) & = & & & 0 & + & 8 & = & 8 5 \left(\right. 1 \left.\right) & & & - & 5 \left(\right. - 1 \left.\right) & = & 5 & & & + & 5 & = & 10$$ The results agree with the right side of the original system, so $$(1 \text{,} 0 \text{,−} 1)$$ is a solution of the system.

snippet: If the augmented matrices of two linear systems are row equivalent, then the two systems have the same solution set.

    <paragraph>If the augmented matrices of two linear systems are row equivalent, then the two systems have the same solution set.</paragraph>

title: Two Fundamental Questions about a Linear System

      <item>If a solution exists, is it the only one; that is, is the solution unique?</item>

title: Example 2
snippet: Example 2: Example 2 Determine if the following system is consistent: x_{1} & - & 2 x_{2} & + & x_{3} & = & 0 & & 2 x_{2} & - & 8 x_{3} & = & 8 5 x_{1} & & & - & 5 x_{3} & = & 10 Solution This is the system from Example 1. Suppose that we...
body_xml:
<example number="2">
    <heading level="2">Example 2</heading>
    <paragraph>Determine if the following system is consistent:</paragraph>
    <paragraph>$$x_{1} & - & 2 x_{2} & + & x_{3} & = & 0 & & 2 x_{2} & - & 8 x_{3} & = & 8 5 x_{1} & & & - & 5 x_{3} & = & 10$$</paragraph>
    <heading level="3">Solution</heading>
    <paragraph>This is the system from Example 1. Suppose that we have performed the row operations necessary to obtain the triangular form</paragraph>
    <paragraph>$$x_{1} & - & 2 x_{2} & + & x_{3} & = & 0 & & x_{2} & - & 4 x_{3} & = & 4 & & & & x_{3} & = & - 1 \begin{bmatrix} 1 & - 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & - 4 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & - 1 \end{bmatrix}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>At this point, we know $$x_{3}$$ . Were we to substitute the value of $$x_{3}$$ into equation 2, we could compute $$x_{2}$$ and hence could determine $$x_{1}$$ from equation 1. So a solution exists; the system is consistent. (In fact, $$x_{2}$$ is uniquely determined by equation 2 since $$x_{3}$$ has only one possible value, and $$x_{1}$$ is therefore uniquely determined by equation 1. So the solution is unique.)</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Example 3
snippet: Example 3: Example 3 Determine if the following system is consistent: (5) & & x_{2} & - & 4 x_{3} & = & 8 2 x_{1} & - & 3 x_{2} & + & 2 x_{3} & = & 1 4 x_{1} & - & 8 x_{2} & + & 12 x_{3} & = & 1 Solution The augmented matrix is...
body_xml: Example 3 Determine if the following system is consistent: (5) $$& & x_{2} & - & 4 x_{3} & = & 8 2 x_{1} & - & 3 x_{2} & + & 2 x_{3} & = & 1 4 x_{1} & - & 8 x_{2} & + & 12 x_{3} & = & 1$$ Solution The augmented matrix is $$\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 & - 4 & 8 \\ 2 & - 3 & 2 & 1 \\ 4 & - 8 & 12 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$$ To obtain an $$x_{1}$$ in the first equation, interchange rows $$1$$ and $$2$$ : $$\begin{bmatrix} 2 & - 3 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & - 4 & 8 \\ 4 & - 8 & 12 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$$ To eliminate the $$4x_{1}$$ term in the third equation, add $$- 2$$ times row $$1$$ to row $$3$$ : (6) $$\begin{bmatrix} 2 & - 3 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & - 4 & 8 \\ 0 & - 2 & 8 & - 1 \end{bmatrix}$$ Next, use the $$x_{2}$$ term in the second equation to eliminate the $$- 2x_{2}$$ term from the third equation. Add $$2$$ times row $$2$$ to row $$3$$ : (7) $$\begin{bmatrix} 2 & - 3 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & - 4 & 8 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 15 \end{bmatrix}$$ The augmented matrix is now in triangular form. To interpret it correctly, go back to equation notation: (8) $$2 x_{1} & - & 3 x_{2} & + & 2 x_{3} & = & 1 & & x_{2} & - & 4 x_{3} & = & 8 & & & & 0 & = & 15$$ The equation $$0 = 15$$ is a short form of $$0x_{1} + 0x_{2} + 0x_{3} = 15$$ . This system in triangular form obviously has a built-in contradiction. There are no values of $$x_{1} \text{,} x_{2} \text{,} x_{3}$$ that satisfy (8) because the equation $$0 = 15$$ is never true. Since (8) and (5) have the same solution set, the original system is inconsistent (it has no solution).

title: Definition
snippet: Definition: Definition A rectangular matrix is in echelon form (or row echelon form) if it has the following three properties: All nonzero rows are above any rows of all zeros. Each leading entry of a row is in a column to the right of the...
body_xml:
<note type="definition" source_type="definition" title="Definition">
    <heading level="2">Definition</heading>
    <paragraph>A rectangular matrix is in echelon form (or row echelon form) if it has the following three properties:</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>All nonzero rows are above any rows of all zeros.</item>
      <item>Each leading entry of a row is in a column to the right of the leading entry of the row above it.</item>
      <item>All entries in a column below a leading entry are zeros.</item>
    </list>
    <paragraph>If a matrix in echelon form satisfies the following additional conditions, then it is in reduced echelon form (or reduced row echelon form):</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>The leading entry in each nonzero row is $$1$$ .</item>
      <item>Each leading $$1$$ is the only nonzero entry in its column.</item>
    </list>
  </note>

title: Definition
snippet: Definition: Definition A pivot position in a matrix A is a location in A that corresponds to a leading 1 in the reduced echelon form of A . A pivot column is a column of A that contains a pivot position.
body_xml:
<note type="definition" source_type="definition" title="Definition">
    <heading level="2">Definition</heading>
    <paragraph>A pivot position in a matrix $$A$$ is a location in $$A$$ that corresponds to a leading $$1$$ in the reduced echelon form of $$A$$ . A pivot column is a column of $$A$$ that contains a pivot position.</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Example 2
snippet: Example 2: Example 2 Row reduce the matrix A below to echelon form, and locate the pivot columns of A . A = \left[\right. 0 & - 3 & - 6 & 4 & 9 - 1 & - 2 & - 1 & 3 & 1 - 2 & - 3 & 0 & 3 & - 1 1 & 4 & 5 & - 9 & - 7 \left]\right. Solution...
body_xml: Example 2 Row reduce the matrix $$A$$ below to echelon form, and locate the pivot columns of $$A$$ . $$A = \left[\right. 0 & - 3 & - 6 & 4 & 9 - 1 & - 2 & - 1 & 3 & 1 - 2 & - 3 & 0 & 3 & - 1 1 & 4 & 5 & - 9 & - 7 \left]\right.$$ Solution Use the same basic strategy as in Section 1.1. The top of the leftmost nonzero column is the first pivot position. A nonzero entry, or pivot, must be placed in this position. A good choice is to interchange rows $$1$$ and $$4$$ (because the mental computations in the next step will not involve fractions). Create zeros below the pivot, $$1$$ , by adding multiples of the first row to the rows below, and obtain matrix (1) below. The pivot position in the second row must be as far left as possible—namely in the second column. Choose the $$2$$ in this position as the next pivot. (1) Add $$- 5/2$$ times row $$2$$ to row $$3$$ , and add $$3/2$$ times row $$2$$ to row $$4$$ . (2) $$\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 4 & 5 & - 9 & - 7 \\ 0 & 2 & 4 & - 6 & - 6 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & - 5 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$$ The matrix in (2) is different from any encountered in Section 1.1. There is no way to create a leading entry in column $$3!$$ (We can’t use row $$1$$ or $$2$$ because doing so would destroy the echelon arrangement of the leading entries already produced.) However, if we interchange rows $$3$$ and $$4$$ , we can produce a leading entry in column $$4$$ . The matrix is in echelon form and thus reveals that columns $$1$$ , $$2$$ , and $$4$$ of $$A$$ are pivot columns. (3)

title: Example 3
snippet: Example 3: Example 3 Apply elementary row operations to transform the following matrix first into echelon form and then into reduced echelon form: \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 3 & - 6 & 6 & 4 & - 5 \\ 3 & - 7 & 8 & - 5 & 8 & 9 \\ 3 & - 9 & 12 & - 9...
body_xml: Example 3 Apply elementary row operations to transform the following matrix first into echelon form and then into reduced echelon form: $$\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 3 & - 6 & 6 & 4 & - 5 \\ 3 & - 7 & 8 & - 5 & 8 & 9 \\ 3 & - 9 & 12 & - 9 & 6 & 15 \end{bmatrix}$$ Solution Step 1 Begin with the leftmost nonzero column. This is a pivot column. The pivot position is at the top. Step 2 Select a nonzero entry in the pivot column as a pivot. If necessary, interchange rows to move this entry into the pivot position. Interchange rows $$1$$ and $$3$$ . (We could have interchanged rows $$1$$ and $$2$$ instead.) Step 3 Use row replacement operations to create zeros in all positions below the pivot. As a preliminary step, we could divide the top row by the pivot, $$3$$ . But with two $$3’s$$ in column $$1$$ , it is just as easy to add $$- 1$$ times row $$1$$ to row $$2$$ . ﻿﻿Step 4﻿ Cover (or ignore) the row containing the pivot position and cover all rows, if any, above it. Apply steps 1–3 to the submatrix that remains. Repeat the process until there are no more nonzero rows to modify. With row $$1$$ covered, step 1 shows that column $$2$$ is the next pivot column; for step 2, select as a pivot the “top” entry in that column. For step 3, we could insert an optional step of dividing the “top” row of the submatrix by the pivot, $$2$$ . Instead, we add $$- 3/2$$ times the “top” row to the row below. This produces When we cover the row containing the second pivot position for step 4, we are left with a new submatrix having only one row: Steps 1–3 require no work for this submatrix, and we have reached an echelon form of the full matrix. If we want the reduced echelon form, we perform one more step. Step 5 Beginning with the rightmost pivot and working upward and to the left, create zeros above each pivot. If a pivot is not $$1$$ , make it $$1$$ by a scaling operation. The rightmost pivot is in row $$3$$ . Create zeros above it, adding suitable multiples of row $$3$$ to rows $$2$$ and $$1$$ . $$\left[\right. 3 & - 9 & 12 & - 9 & 0 & - 9 0 & 2 & - 4 & 4 & 0 & - 14 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 & 4 \left]\right. \leftarrow \text{Row} 1 + \left(\right. - 6 \left.\right) \cdot \text{row} 3 \leftarrow \text{Row} 2 + \left(\right. - 2 \left.\right) \cdot \text{row} 3$$ The next pivot is in row 2. Scale this row, dividing by the pivot. $$\left[\right. 3 & - 9 & 12 & - 9 & 0 & - 9 0 & 1 & - 2 & 2 & 0 & - 7 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 & 4 \left]\right. \leftarrow \text{Row} \text{scaled} \text{by} \frac{1}{2}$$ Create a zero in column $$2$$ by adding $$9$$ times row $$2$$ to row $$1$$ . $$\left[\right. 3 & 0 & - 6 & 9 & 0 & - 72 0 & 1 & - 2 & 2 & 0 & - 7 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 & 4 \left]\right. \leftarrow \text{Row} 1 + \left(\right. 9 \left.\right) \cdot \text{row} 2$$ Finally, scale row $$1$$ , dividing by the pivot, $$3$$ . $$\left[\right. 1 & 0 & - 2 & 3 & 0 & - 24 0 & 1 & - 2 & 2 & 0 & - 7 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 & 4 \left]\right. \leftarrow \text{Row} \text{scaled} \text{by} \frac{1}{3}$$ This is the reduced echelon form of the original matrix.

title: Example 4
snippet: Example 4: Example 4 Find the general solution of the linear system whose augmented matrix has been reduced to \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 6 & 2 & - 5 & - 2 & - 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & - 8 & - 1 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 & 7 \end{bmatrix} Solution The...
body_xml:
<example number="4">
    <heading level="2">Example 4</heading>
    <paragraph>Find the general solution of the linear system whose augmented matrix has been reduced to</paragraph>
    <paragraph>$$\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 6 & 2 & - 5 & - 2 & - 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & - 8 & - 1 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 & 7 \end{bmatrix}$$</paragraph>
    <heading level="3">Solution</heading>
    <paragraph>The matrix is in echelon form, but we want the reduced echelon form before solving for the basic variables. The row reduction is completed next. The symbol $$\sim$$ before a matrix indicates that the matrix is row equivalent to the preceding matrix.</paragraph>
    <paragraph>$$\left[\right. \begin{matrix}1 & 6 & 2 & - 5 & - 2 & - 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & - 8 & - 1 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 & 7\end{matrix} \left]\right. sim \left[\right. \begin{matrix}1 & 6 & 2 & - 5 & 0 & 10 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & - 8 & 0 & 10 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 & 7\end{matrix} \left]\right. sim \left[\right. \begin{matrix}1 & 6 & 2 & - 5 & 0 & 10 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & - 4 & 0 & 5 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 & 7\end{matrix} \left]\right. sim \left[\right. \begin{matrix}1 & 6 & 0 & 3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & - 4 & 0 & 5 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 & 7\end{matrix} \left]\right.$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>There are five variables because the augmented matrix has six columns. The associated system now is</paragraph>
    <paragraph>(6)</paragraph>
    <paragraph>$$x_{1} & + & 6 x_{2} & & + & 3 x_{4} & & = & 0 & & & x_{3} & - & 4 x_{4} & & = & 5 & & & & & & x_{5} & = & 7$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>The pivot columns of the matrix are $$1$$ , $$3$$ , and $$5$$ , so the basic variables are $$x_{1}$$ , $$x_{3}$$ , and $$x_{5}$$ . The remaining variables, $$x_{2}$$ and $$x_{4}$$ , must be free. Solve for the basic variables to obtain the general solution:</paragraph>
    <paragraph>(7)</paragraph>
    <paragraph>$$\left{\begin{matrix} x_{1} = - 6 x_{2} - 3 x_{4} \\ x_{2} \text{is} \text{free} \\ x_{3} = 5 + 4 x_{4} \\ x_{4} \text{is} \text{free} \\ x_{5} = 7 \end{matrix}\right$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Note that the value of $$x_{5}$$ is already fixed by the third equation in system (6).</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Example 5
snippet: Example 5: Example 5 Determine the existence and uniqueness of the solutions to the system & & 3 x_{2} & - & 6 x_{3} & + & 6 x_{4} & + & 4 x_{5} & = & - 5 3 x_{1} & - & 7 x_{2} & + & 8 x_{3} & - & 5 x_{4} & + & 8 x_{5} & = & 9 3 x_{1} & -...
body_xml:
<example number="5">
    <heading level="2">Example 5</heading>
    <paragraph>Determine the existence and uniqueness of the solutions to the system</paragraph>
    <paragraph>$$& & 3 x_{2} & - & 6 x_{3} & + & 6 x_{4} & + & 4 x_{5} & = & - 5 3 x_{1} & - & 7 x_{2} & + & 8 x_{3} & - & 5 x_{4} & + & 8 x_{5} & = & 9 3 x_{1} & - & 9 x_{2} & + & 12 x_{3} & - & 9 x_{4} & + & 6 x_{5} & = & 15$$</paragraph>
    <heading level="3">Solution</heading>
    <paragraph>The augmented matrix of this system was row reduced in Example 3 to</paragraph>
    <paragraph>(8)</paragraph>
    <paragraph>$$\begin{bmatrix} 3 & - 9 & 1 2 & - 9 & 6 & 1 5 \\ 0 & 2 & - 4 & 4 & 2 & - 6 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 & 4 \end{bmatrix}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>The basic variables are $$x_{1}$$ , $$x_{2}$$ , and $$x_{5}$$ ; the free variables are $$x_{3}$$ and $$x_{4}$$ . There is no equation such as $$0 = 1$$ that would indicate an inconsistent system, so we could use back-substitution to find a solution. But the existence of a solution is already clear in (8). Also, the solution is not unique because there are free variables. Each different choice of $$x_{3}$$ and $$x_{4}$$ determines a different solution. Thus the system has infinitely many solutions.</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Theorem 2
snippet: Theorem 2: Theorem 2 Existence and Uniqueness Theorem A linear system is consistent if and only if the rightmost column of the augmented matrix is not a pivot column—that is, if and only if an echelon form of the augmented matrix has no...
body_xml:
<note type="procedure" source_type="procedure" title="Theorem 2">
    <heading level="2">Theorem 2</heading>
    <heading level="3">Existence and Uniqueness Theorem</heading>
    <paragraph>A linear system is consistent if and only if the rightmost column of the augmented matrix is not a pivot column—that is, if and only if an echelon form of the augmented matrix has no row of the form</paragraph>
    <paragraph>$$[ 0 \hdots 0 b ] \text{with} b \text{nonzero}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>If a linear system is consistent, then the solution set contains either (i) a unique solution, when there are no free variables, or (ii) infinitely many solutions, when there is at least one free variable.</paragraph>
  </note>

snippet: Algebraic Properties of ℝn: Algebraic Properties of ℝn For all \mathbf{u} \text{,} \mathbf{v} \text{,} \mathbf{w} in \mathbb{R}^{n} and all scalars c and d : \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{v} + \mathbf{u} \left(\right. \mathbf{u} +...
body_xml:
<note type="theorem" source_type="theorem_key" title="Algebraic Properties of ℝn">
    <heading level="2">Algebraic Properties of ℝn</heading>
    <paragraph>For all $$\mathbf{u} \text{,} \mathbf{v} \text{,} \mathbf{w}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ and all scalars $$c$$ and $$d$$ :</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>$$\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{v} + \mathbf{u}$$</item>
      <item>$$\left(\right. \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v} \left.\right) + \mathbf{w} = \mathbf{u} + \left(\right. \mathbf{v} + \mathbf{w} \left.\right)$$</item>
      <item>$$\mathbf{u} + 0 = 0 + \mathbf{u} = \mathbf{u}$$</item>
      <item>$$\mathbf{u} + ( - \mathbf{u}) = - \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{u} = 0$$ , where $$- \mathbf{u}$$ denotes $$\left(\right. - 1 \left.\right) \mathbf{u}$$</item>
      <item>$$c \left(\right. \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v} \left.\right) = c \mathbf{u} + c \mathbf{v}$$</item>
      <item>$$\left(\right. c + d \left.\right) \mathbf{u} = c \mathbf{u} + d \mathbf{u}$$</item>
      <item>$$c \left(\right. d \mathbf{u} \left.\right) = \left(\right. c d \left.\right) \mathbf{u}$$</item>
      <item>$$1 \mathbf{u} = \mathbf{u}$$</item>
    </list>
  </note>

body_xml: Example 4 Figure 8 identifies selected linear combinations of $$\mathbf{v}_{1} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} {- 1} \\ 1 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ and $$\mathbf{v}_{2} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 2 \\ 1 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ . (Note that sets of parallel grid lines are drawn through integer multiples of $$\mathbf{v}_{1}$$ and $$\mathbf{v}_{2}$$ .) Estimate the linear combinations of $$\mathbf{v}_{1}$$ and $$\mathbf{v}_{2}$$ that generate the vectors $$\mathbf{u}$$ and $$\mathbf{w}$$ . Click here for interactive version of Figure 8 Solution The parallelogram rule shows that $$\mathbf{u}$$ is the sum of $$3\mathbf{v}_{1}$$ and $$- 2\mathbf{v}_{2}$$ ; that is, $$\mathbf{u} = 3 \mathbf{v}_{1} - 2 \mathbf{v}_{2}$$ This expression for $$\mathbf{u}$$ can be interpreted as instructions for traveling from the origin to $$\mathbf{u}$$ along two straight paths. First, travel 3 units in the $$\mathbf{v}_{1}$$ direction to $$3\mathbf{v}_{1}$$ , and then travel $$- 2$$ units in the $$\mathbf{v}_{2}$$ direction (parallel to the line through $$\mathbf{v}_{2}$$ and $$0$$ ). Next, although the vector $$\mathbf{w}$$ is not on a grid line, $$\mathbf{w}$$ appears to be about halfway between two pairs of grid lines, at the vertex of a parallelogram determined by $$(5/2)\mathbf{v}_{1}$$ and $$( - 1/2)\mathbf{v}_{2}$$ . (See Figure 9.) Thus a reasonable estimate for $$\mathbf{w}$$ is $$\mathbf{w} = \frac{5}{2} \mathbf{v}_{1} - \frac{1}{2} \mathbf{v}_{2}$$

title: Example 5
snippet: Example 5: Example 5 Let \mathbf{a}_{1} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 1 \\ {- 2} \\ {- 5} \end{array} \right\rbrack , \mathbf{a}_{2} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 5 \\ 6 \end{bmatrix} , and \mathbf{b} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 7 \\ 4 \\...
body_xml:
<example number="5">
    <heading level="2">Example 5</heading>
    <paragraph>Let $$\mathbf{a}_{1} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 1 \\ {- 2} \\ {- 5} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , $$\mathbf{a}_{2} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 5 \\ 6 \end{bmatrix}$$ , and $$\mathbf{b} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 7 \\ 4 \\ {- 3} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ . Determine whether $$\mathbf{b}$$ can be generated (or written) as a linear combination of $$\mathbf{a}_{1}$$ and $$\mathbf{a}_{2}$$ . That is, determine whether weights $$x_{1}$$ and $$x_{2}$$ exist such that</paragraph>
    <paragraph>(1)</paragraph>
    <paragraph>$$x_{1} \mathbf{a}_{1} + x_{2} \mathbf{a}_{2} = \mathbf{b}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>If vector equation (1) has a solution, find it.</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Click here to explore the problem geometrically</paragraph>
    <heading level="3">Solution</heading>
    <paragraph>Use the definitions of scalar multiplication and vector addition to rewrite the vector equation</paragraph>
    <paragraph>$$x_{1} \underset{}{\left[\right. \begin{matrix}1 \\ - 2 \\ - 5\end{matrix} \left]\right.} & + & x_{2} \underset{}{\left[\right. \begin{matrix}2 \\ 5 \\ 6\end{matrix} \left]\right.} & = & \left[\right. \begin{matrix}7 \\ 4 \\ - 3\end{matrix} \left]\right. \uparrow & & \uparrow & & \uparrow \mathbf{a}_{1} & & \mathbf{a}_{2} & & \mathbf{a}_{3}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>which is the same as</paragraph>
    <paragraph>$$\begin{bmatrix} x_{1} \\ - 2 x_{1} \\ - 5 x_{1} \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} 2 x_{2} \\ 5 x_{2} \\ 6 x_{2} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 7 \\ 4 \\ - 3 \end{bmatrix}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>and</paragraph>
    <paragraph>(2)</paragraph>
    <paragraph>$$\begin{bmatrix} x_{1} + 2 x_{2} \\ - 2 x_{1} + 5 x_{2} \\ - 5 x_{1} + 6 x_{2} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 7 \\ 4 \\ - 3 \end{bmatrix}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>The vectors on the left and right sides of (2) are equal if and only if their corresponding entries are both equal. That is, $$x_{1}$$ and $$x_{2}$$ make the vector equation (1) true if and only if $$x_{1}$$ and $$x_{2}$$ satisfy the system</paragraph>
    <paragraph>(3)</paragraph>
    <paragraph>$$x_{1} & + & 2 x_{2} & = & 7 - 2 x_{1} & + & 5 x_{2} & = & 4 - 5 x_{1} & + & 6 x_{2} & = & - 3$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>To solve this system, row reduce the augmented matrix of the system as follows:3</paragraph>
    <paragraph>$$\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 7 \\ - 2 & 5 & 4 \\ - 5 & 6 & - 3 \end{bmatrix} ∼ \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 7 \\ 0 & 9 & 1 8 \\ 0 & 1 6 & 3 2 \end{bmatrix} ∼ \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 7 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 16 & 32 \end{bmatrix} ∼ \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>The solution of (3) is $$x_{1} = 3$$ and $$x_{2} = 2$$ . Hence $$\mathbf{b}$$ is a linear combination of $$\mathbf{a}_{1}$$ and $$\mathbf{a}_{2}$$ , with weights $$x_{1} = 3$$ and $$x_{2} = 2$$ . That is,</paragraph>
    <paragraph>$$3 \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ - 2 \\ - 5 \end{bmatrix} + 2 \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 5 \\ 6 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 7 \\ 4 \\ - 3 \end{bmatrix}$$</paragraph>
  </example>

snippet: A vector equation x_{1} \mathbf{a}_{1} + x_{2} \mathbf{a}_{2} + \hdots + x_{n} \mathbf{a}_{n} = \mathbf{b} has the same solution set as the linear system whose augmented matrix is (5) \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{a}_{1} & \mathbf{a}_{2} &...
body_xml:
<note type="theorem" source_type="theorem_key">
    <paragraph>A vector equation</paragraph>
    <paragraph>$$x_{1} \mathbf{a}_{1} + x_{2} \mathbf{a}_{2} + \hdots + x_{n} \mathbf{a}_{n} = \mathbf{b}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>has the same solution set as the linear system whose augmented matrix is</paragraph>
    <paragraph>(5)</paragraph>
    <paragraph>$$\begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{a}_{1} & \mathbf{a}_{2} & \hdots & \mathbf{a}_{n} & \mathbf{b} \end{bmatrix}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>In particular, $$\mathbf{b}$$ can be generated by a linear combination of $$\mathbf{a}_{1} \text{,…,} \textbf{}\mathbf{a}_{n}$$ if and only if there exists a solution to the linear system corresponding to the matrix (5).</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Definition
snippet: Definition: Definition If \mathbf{v}_{1} \text{,…,} \mathbf{v}_{p} are in \mathbb{R}^{n} , then the set of all linear combinations of \mathbf{v}_{1} \text{,…,} \mathbf{v}_{p} is denoted by \text{Span\{} \mathbf{v}1 \text{,…,}...
body_xml:
<note type="definition" source_type="definition" title="Definition">
    <heading level="2">Definition</heading>
    <paragraph>If $$\mathbf{v}_{1} \text{,…,} \mathbf{v}_{p}$$ are in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ , then the set of all linear combinations of $$\mathbf{v}_{1} \text{,…,} \mathbf{v}_{p}$$ is denoted by $$\text{Span\{} \mathbf{v}1 \text{,…,} \mathbf{v}_{p} \text{\}}$$ and is called the subset of $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{\mathbf{\mathit{n}}}$$ spanned by (or generated) $$\mathbf{v}_{1} \text{,…,} \mathbf{v}_{p}$$ . That is, $$\text{Span\{} \mathbf{v}_{1} \text{,…,} \mathbf{v}_{p} \text{\}}$$ is the collection of all vectors that can be written in the form</paragraph>
    <paragraph>$$c_{1} \mathbf{v}_{1} + c_{2} \mathbf{v}_{2} + \hdots + c_{p} \mathbf{v}_{p}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>with $$c_{1} \text{,…,} c_{p}$$ scalars.</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Example 6
snippet: Example 6: Example 6 Let \mathbf{a}_{1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ - 2 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix} , \mathbf{a}_{2} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 5 \\ {- 13} \\ {- 3} \end{array} \right\rbrack, and \mathbf{b} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} {- 3} \\...
body_xml:
<example number="6">
    <heading level="2">Example 6</heading>
    <paragraph>Let $$\mathbf{a}_{1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ - 2 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix} ,$$ $$\mathbf{a}_{2} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 5 \\ {- 13} \\ {- 3} \end{array} \right\rbrack,$$ and $$\mathbf{b} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} {- 3} \\ 8 \\ 1 \end{array} \right\rbrack.$$ Then $$\text{Span} \{\mathbf{a}_{1} \text{,} \mathbf{a}_{2}\}$$ is a plane through the origin in $$\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ . Is $$\mathbf{b}$$ in that plane?</paragraph>
    <heading level="3">Solution</heading>
    <paragraph>Does the equation $$x_{1}\mathbf{a}_{1} + x_{2}\mathbf{a}_{2} = \mathbf{b}$$ have a solution? To answer this, row reduce the augmented matrix $$\left\lbrack \begin{array}{lll} \textbf{a}_{1} & \textbf{a}_{2} & \textbf{b} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ :</paragraph>
    <paragraph>$$\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 5 & - 3 \\ - 2 & - 13 & 8 \\ 3 & - 3 & 1 \end{bmatrix} ∼ \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 5 & - 3 \\ 0 & - 3 & 2 \\ 0 & - 18 & 10 \end{bmatrix} ∼ \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 5 & - 3 \\ 0 & - 3 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & - 2 \end{bmatrix}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>The third equation is $$0 = - 2$$ , which shows that the system has no solution. The vector equation $$x_{1}\mathbf{a}_{1} + x_{2}\mathbf{a}_{2} = \mathbf{b}$$ has no solution, and so $$\mathbf{b}$$ is not in $$\text{Span\{} \mathbf{a}_{1} \text{,} \mathbf{a}_{2} \text{\}}$$ .</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Example 7
snippet: Example 7: Example 7 A company manufactures two products. For $$\$1.00 worth of product B, the company spends \$.45 on materials, \$.25 on labor, and \$.15 on overhead. For \$1.00 worth of product C, the company spends \$.40 on materials,...
body_xml:
<example number="7">
    <heading level="2">Example 7</heading>
    <paragraph>A company manufactures two products. For $$\$1.00$$ worth of product B, the company spends $$\$.45$$ on materials, $$\$.25$$ on labor, and $$\$.15$$ on overhead. For $$\$1.00$$ worth of product C, the company spends $$\$.40$$ on materials, $$\$.30$$ on labor, and $$\$.15$$ on overhead. Let</paragraph>
    <paragraph>$$\mathbf{b} = \begin{bmatrix} .45 \\ .25 \\ .15 \end{bmatrix} \text{and} \mathbf{c} = \begin{bmatrix} .40 \\ .30 \\ .15 \end{bmatrix}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Then $$\mathbf{b}$$ and $$\mathbf{c}$$ represent the “costs per dollar of income” for the two products.</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>What economic interpretation can be given to the vector $$100 \mathbf{b} ?$$</item>
      <item>Suppose the company wishes to manufacture $$x_{1}$$ dollars worth of product B and $$x_{2}$$ dollars worth of product C. Give a vector that describes the various costs the company will have (for materials, labor, and overhead).</item>
    </list>
    <heading level="3">Solution</heading>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>Compute</item>
    </list>
    <paragraph>$$100 \mathbf{b} = 100 \begin{bmatrix} .45 \\ .25 \\ .15 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 45 \\ 25 \\ 15 \end{bmatrix}$$</paragraph>
    <list type="unordered">
      <item>The vector $$100\mathbf{b}$$ lists the various costs for producing $$\$100$$ worth of product B—namely $$\$45$$ for materials, $$\$25$$ for labor, and $$\$15$$ for overhead.</item>
    </list>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>The costs of manufacturing $$x_{1}$$ dollars worth of B are given by the vector $$x_{1}\mathbf{b}$$ , and the costs of manufacturing $$x_{2}$$ dollars worth of C are given by $$x_{2}\mathbf{c}$$ . Hence the total costs for both products are given by the vector $$x_{1}\mathbf{b} + x_{2}\mathbf{c}$$ .</item>
    </list>
  </example>

snippet: Definition: Definition If A is an m \times n matrix, with columns \mathbf{a}_{1} \text{,…} \text{,} \mathbf{a}_{n} , and if \mathbf{x} is in \mathbb{R}^{n} , then the product of A and \mathbf{x} , denoted by A\mathbf{x} , is the linear...
body_xml:
<note type="definition" source_type="definition" title="Definition">
    <heading level="2">Definition</heading>
    <paragraph>If $$A$$ is an $$m \times n$$ matrix, with columns $$\mathbf{a}_{1} \text{,…} \text{,} \mathbf{a}_{n}$$ , and if $$\mathbf{x}$$ is in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ , then the product of $$A$$ and $$\mathbf{x}$$ , denoted by $$A\mathbf{x}$$ , is the linear combination of the columns of $$A$$ using the corresponding entries in $$x$$ as weights; that is,</paragraph>
    <paragraph>$$A \mathbf{x} = \left[\right. \mathbf{a}_{1} \mathbf{a}_{2} \hdots \mathbf{a}_{n} \left]\right. \left[\right. x_{1} \vdots x_{n} \left]\right. = x_{1} \mathbf{a}_{1} + x_{2} \mathbf{a}_{2} + \hdots + x_{n} \mathbf{a}_{n}$$</paragraph>
  </note>

<example number="3">

    <paragraph>Let $$A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 & 4 \\ {- 4} & 2 & {- 6} \\ {- 3} & {- 2} & {- 7} \end{bmatrix}$$ and $$\mathbf{b} = \begin{bmatrix} b_{1} \\ b_{2} \\ b_{3} \end{bmatrix}.$$ Is the equation $$A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$$ consistent for all possible $$b_{1} , b_{2} , b_{3} ?$$</paragraph>

    <paragraph>Row reduce the augmented matrix for $$A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$$ :</paragraph>

    <paragraph>The third entry in column $$4$$ equals $$b_{1}-\frac{1}{2}b_{2} + b_{3}$$ . The equation $$A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$$ is not consistent for every $$\mathbf{b}$$ because some choices of $$\mathbf{b}$$ can make $$b_{1}-\frac{1}{2}b_{2} + b_{3}$$ nonzero.</paragraph>
  </example>

      <item>The columns of $$A$$ span $$\mathbb{R}^{m}$$ .</item>
      <item>$$A$$ has a pivot position in every row.</item>
    </list>
  </note>

    <paragraph>From the definition,</paragraph>
    <paragraph>(7)﻿</paragraph>
    <paragraph>$$\begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}2 & 3 & 4 \\ - 1 & 5 & - 3 \\ 6 & - 2 & 8\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}x_{1} \\ x_{2} \\ x_{3}\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} & = x_{1} \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}2 \\ - 1 \\ 6\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} + x_{2} \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}3 \\ 5 \\ - 2\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} + x_{3} \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}4 \\ - 3 \\ 8\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} & = \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}2 x_{1} \\ - x_{1} \\ 6 x_{1}\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}3 x_{2} \\ 5 x_{2} \\ - 2 x_{2}\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}4 x_{3} \\ - 3 x_{3} \\ 8 x_{3}\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} & = \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}2 x_{1} + 3 x_{2} + 4 x_{3} \\ - x_{1} + 5 x_{2} - 3 x_{3} \\ 6 x_{1} - 2 x_{2} + 8 x_{3}\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>The first entry in the product $$A\mathbf{x}$$ is a sum of products (sometimes called a dot product), using the first row of $$A$$ and the entries in $$\mathbf{x}$$ . That is,</paragraph>
    <paragraph>$$\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 3 & 4 \\ & & \\ & & \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x_{1} \\ x_{2} \\ x_{3} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 x_{1} + 3 x_{2} + 4 x_{3} \\ \\ \end{bmatrix}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>This matrix shows how to compute the first entry in $$A\mathbf{x}$$ directly, without writing down all the calculations shown in (7). Similarly, the second entry in $$A\mathbf{x}$$ can be calculated at once by multiplying the entries in the second row of $$A$$ by the corresponding entries in $$\mathbf{x}$$ and then summing the resulting products:</paragraph>
    <paragraph>$$\begin{bmatrix} & & \\ - 1 & 5 & - 3 \\ & & \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x_{1} \\ x_{2} \\ x_{3} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \\ - x_{1} + 5 x_{2} - 3 x_{3} \\ \end{bmatrix}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Likewise, the third entry in $$A\mathbf{x}$$ can be calculated from the third row of $$A$$ and the entries in $$\mathbf{x}$$ .</paragraph>
  </example>

snippet: The homogeneous equation A\mathbf{x} = 0 has a nontrivial solution if and only if the equation has at least one free variable.
body_xml:
<note type="theorem" source_type="theorem_key">
    <paragraph>The homogeneous equation $$A\mathbf{x} = 0$$ has a nontrivial solution if and only if the equation has at least one free variable.</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Example 1
snippet: Example 1: Example 1 Determine if the following homogeneous system has a nontrivial solution. Then describe the solution set. 3 x_{1} & + & 5 x_{2} & - & 4 x_{3} & = & 0 - 3 x_{1} & - & 2 x_{2} & + & 4 x_{3} & = & 0 6 x_{1} & + & x_{2} & -...
body_xml: Example 1 Determine if the following homogeneous system has a nontrivial solution. Then describe the solution set. $$3 x_{1} & + & 5 x_{2} & - & 4 x_{3} & = & 0 - 3 x_{1} & - & 2 x_{2} & + & 4 x_{3} & = & 0 6 x_{1} & + & x_{2} & - & 8 x_{3} & = & 0$$ Solution Let $$A$$ be the matrix of coefficients of the system and row reduce the augmented matrix $$\lbrack A 0\rbrack$$ to echelon form: $$\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 5 & - 4 & 0 \\ - 3 & - 2 & 4 & 0 \\ 6 & 1 & - 8 & 0 \end{bmatrix} ∼ \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 5 & - 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & - 9 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} ∼ \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 5 & - 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$$ Since $$x_{3}$$ is a free variable, $$A\mathbf{x} = 0$$ has nontrivial solutions (one for each nonzero choice of $$x_{3}$$ ). To describe the solution set, continue the row reduction of $$\lbrack A 0\rbrack$$ to reduced echelon form: $$\begin{bmatrix} 1 & & & & 0 & & - \frac{4}{3} & & & & 0 \\ 0 & & & & 1 & & 0 & & & & 0 \\ 0 & & & & 0 & & 0 & & & & 0 \end{bmatrix} x_{1} & & & - & \frac{4}{3} x_{3} & = & 0 & & x_{2} & & & = & 0 & & & & 0 & = & 0$$ Solve for the basic variables $$x_{1}$$ and $$x_{2}$$ and obtain $$x_{1} = \frac{4}{3}x_{3}$$ , $$x_{2} = 0$$ , with $$x_{3}$$ free. As a vector, the general solution of $$A\mathbf{x} = 0$$ has the form $$\mathbf{x} = \begin{bmatrix} x_{1} \\ x_{2} \\ x_{3} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{4}{3} x_{3} \\ 0 \\ x_{3} \end{bmatrix} = x_{3} \begin{bmatrix} \frac{4}{3} \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = x_{3} \mathbf{v} , \text{where} \mathbf{v} = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{4}{3} \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$$ Here $$x_{3}$$ is factored out of the expression for the general solution vector. This shows that every solution of $$A\mathbf{x} = 0$$ in this case is a scalar multiple of $$\mathbf{v}$$ . The trivial solution is obtained by choosing $$x_{3} = 0.$$ Geometrically, the solution set is a line through $$0$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ . See Figure 1. Click here for an Interactive version of Figure 1

title: Example 2
snippet: Example 2: Example 2 A single linear equation can be treated as a very simple system of equations. Describe all solutions of the homogeneous “system” (1) 10 x_{1} - 3 x_{2} - 2 x_{3} = 0 Solution There is no need for matrix notation. Solve...
body_xml: Example 2 A single linear equation can be treated as a very simple system of equations. Describe all solutions of the homogeneous “system” (1) $$10 x_{1} - 3 x_{2} - 2 x_{3} = 0$$ Solution There is no need for matrix notation. Solve for the basic variable $$x_{1}$$ in terms of the free variables. The general solution is $$x_{1} = .3x_{2} + .2x_{3}$$ , with $$x_{2}$$ and $$x_{3}$$ free. As a vector, the general solution is (2) $$\textbf{x} = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}x_{1} \\ x_{2} \\ x_{3}\end{matrix} \left]\right. & = & \left[\right. \begin{matrix}.3 x_{2} + .2 x_{2} \\ x_{2} \\ x_{3}\end{matrix} \left]\right. = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}.3 x_{2} \\ x_{2} \\ 0\end{matrix} \left]\right. + \left[\right. \begin{matrix}.2 x 3 \\ 0 \\ x_{3}\end{matrix} \left]\right. & = & x_{2} \left[\right. \begin{matrix}.3 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{matrix} \left]\right. + x_{3} \left[\right. \begin{matrix}.2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{matrix} \left]\right. ( \text{with} x_{2} , x_{ \text{3} } \text{free} ) & & \begin{matrix} & \overset{ \uparrow}{ \textbf{u}} & & \end{matrix} \overset{ \uparrow}{ \textbf{v}}$$ This calculation shows that every solution of (1) is a linear combination of the vectors $$\mathbf{u}$$ and $$\mathbf{v}$$ , shown in (2). That is, the solution set is $$\text{Span} \{\mathbf{u} \text{,} \mathbf{v}\}$$ . Since neither $$\mathbf{u}$$ nor $$\mathbf{v}$$ is a scalar multiple of the other, the solution set is a plane through the origin. See Figure 2.

title: Example 3
snippet: Example 3: Example 3 Describe all solutions of A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b} , where A = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 5 & - 4 \\ - 3 & - 2 & 4 \\ 6 & 1 & - 8 \end{bmatrix} \text{and} \mathbf{b} = \begin{bmatrix} 7 \\ - 1 \\ - 4 \end{bmatrix} Solution...
body_xml:
<example number="3">
    <heading level="2">Example 3</heading>
    <paragraph>Describe all solutions of $$A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$$ , where</paragraph>
    <paragraph>$$A = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 5 & - 4 \\ - 3 & - 2 & 4 \\ 6 & 1 & - 8 \end{bmatrix} \text{and} \mathbf{b} = \begin{bmatrix} 7 \\ - 1 \\ - 4 \end{bmatrix}$$</paragraph>
    <heading level="3">Solution</heading>
    <paragraph>Here $$A$$ is the matrix of coefficients from Example 1. Row operations on $$\lbrack A \mathbf{b}\rbrack$$ produce</paragraph>
    <paragraph>$$\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 5 & - 4 & 7 \\ - 3 & - 2 & 4 & - 1 \\ 6 & 1 & - 8 & - 4 \end{bmatrix} ∼ \begin{bmatrix} 1 & & 0 & - \frac{4}{3} & - 1 \\ 0 & & 1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & & 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} , x_{1} & & & - & \frac{4}{3} x_{3} & = & - 1 & & x_{2} & & & = & 2 & & & & 0 & = & 0$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Thus $$x_{1} = - 1 + \frac{4}{3}x^{3}$$ , $$x_{2} = 2$$ , and $$x_{3}$$ is free. As a vector, the general solution of $$A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$$ has the form</paragraph>
    <paragraph>$$\text{x} & = & \left[\right. \begin{matrix}x_{1} \\ x_{2} \\ x_{3}\end{matrix} \left]\right. & = & \left[\right. \begin{matrix}- 1 + \frac{4}{3} x_{3} \\ 2 \\ x_{3}\end{matrix} \left]\right. & = & \left[\right. \begin{matrix}- 1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{matrix} \left]\right. & + & \left[\right. \begin{matrix}\frac{4}{3} x_{3} \\ 0 \\ x_{3}\end{matrix} \left]\right. & = & \left[\right. \begin{matrix}- 1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{matrix} \left]\right. & + & x_{3} \left[\right. \begin{matrix}\frac{4}{3} \\ 0 \\ 1\end{matrix} \left]\right. & & & & & & & & & & \overset{\uparrow}{ \text{p} } & & \overset{\uparrow}{ \text{v} }$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>The equation $$\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{p} + x_{3}\mathbf{v}$$ , or, writing $$t$$ as a general parameter,</paragraph>
    <paragraph>(3)</paragraph>
    <paragraph>$$\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{p} + t \mathbf{v} \left(\right. t \text{in} \mathbb{R} \left.\right)$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>describes the solution set of $$A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$$ in parametric vector form. Recall from Example 1 that the solution set of $$A\mathbf{x} = 0$$ has the parametric vector equation</paragraph>
    <paragraph>(4)</paragraph>
    <paragraph>$$\mathbf{x} = t \mathbf{v} \left(\right. t \text{in} \mathbb{R} \left.\right)$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>[with the same $$\mathbf{v}$$ that appears in (3)]. Thus the solutions of $$A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$$ are obtained by adding the vector $$\mathbf{p}$$ to the solutions of $$A\mathbf{x} = 0$$ . The vector $$\mathbf{p}$$ itself is just one particular solution of $$A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$$ [corresponding to $$t = 0$$ in (3)].</paragraph>
  </example>

snippet: Theorem 6: Theorem 6 Suppose the equation A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b} is consistent for some given \mathbf{b} , and let \mathbf{p} be a solution. Then the solution set of A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b} is the set of all vectors of the form...

<note type="procedure" source_type="procedure" title="Theorem 6">
    <heading level="2">Theorem 6</heading>
    <paragraph>Suppose the equation $$A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$$ is consistent for some given $$\mathbf{b}$$ , and let $$\mathbf{p}$$ be a solution. Then the solution set of $$A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$$ is the set of all vectors of the form $$\mathbf{w} = \mathbf{p} + \mathbf{v}_{h}$$ , where $$\mathbf{v}_{h}$$ is any solution of the homogeneous equation $$A\mathbf{x} = 0$$ .</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Example 1
snippet: Example 1: Example 1 Suppose an economy consists of the Coal, Electric (power), and Steel sectors, and the output of each sector is distributed among the various sectors as shown in Table 1, where the entries in a column represent the...
body_xml: Example 1 Suppose an economy consists of the Coal, Electric (power), and Steel sectors, and the output of each sector is distributed among the various sectors as shown in Table 1, where the entries in a column represent the fractional parts of a sector’s total output. The second column of Table 1, for instance, says that the total output of the Electric sector is divided as follows: $$40\%$$ to Coal, $$50\%$$ to Steel, and the remaining $$10\%$$ to Electric. (Electric treats this $$10\%$$ as an expense it incurs in order to operate its business.) Since all output must be taken into account, the decimal fractions in each column must sum to $$1$$ . Denote the prices (in dollar values) of the total annual outputs of the Coal, Electric, and Steel sectors by $$p_{ \text{C} }$$ , $$p_{ \text{E} }$$ , and $$p_{ \text{S} }$$ , respectively. If possible, find equilibrium prices that make each sector’s income match its expenditures. Solution A sector looks down a column to see where its output goes, and it looks across a row to see what it needs as inputs. For instance, the first row of Table 1 says that Coal receives (and pays for) $$40\%$$ of the Electric output and $$60\%$$ of the Steel output. Since the respective values of the total outputs are $$p_{ \text{E} }$$ and $$p_{ \text{S} }$$ , Coal must spend $$.4p_{ \text{E} }$$ dollars for its share of Electric’s output and $$.6p_{ \text{S} }$$ for its share of Steel’s output. Thus Coal’s total expenses are $$.4p_{ \text{E} } + .6p_{ \text{S} }$$ . To make Coal’s income, $$p_{ \text{C} }$$ , equal to its expenses, we want (1) $$p_{ \text{C} } = .4 p_{ \text{E} } + .6 p_{ \text{S} }$$ The second row of the exchange table shows that the Electric sector spends $$.6p_{ \text{C} }$$ for coal, $$.1p_{ \text{E} }$$ for electricity, and $$.2p_{ \text{S} }$$ for steel. Hence the income/expense requirement for Electric is (2) $$p_{ \text{E} } = .6 p_{ \text{C} } + .1 p_{ \text{E} } + .2 p_{ \text{S} }$$ Finally, the third row of the exchange table leads to the final requirement: (3) $$p_{ \text{S} } = .4 p_{ \text{C} } + .5 p_{ \text{E} } + .2 p_{ \text{S} }$$ To solve the system of equations (1), (2), and (3), move all the unknowns to the left sides of the equations and combine like terms. [For instance, on the left side of (2), write $$p_{ \text{E} } - .1p_{ \text{E} }$$ as $$.9p_{ \text{E} }$$ .] $$p_{ \text{C} } & - & .4 p_{ \text{E} } & - & .6 p_{ \text{S} } & = & 0 - .6 p_{ \text{C} } & + & .9 p_{ \text{E} } & - & .2 p_{ \text{S} } & = & 0 - .4 p_{ \text{C} } & - & .5 p_{ \text{E} } & + & .8 p_{ \text{S} } & = & 0$$ Row reduction is next. For simplicity here, decimals are rounded to two places. $$\begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}1 & - . 4 & - . 6 & 0 \\ - .6 & . 9 & - . 2 & 0 \\ - .4 & - . 5 & . 8 & 0\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} & sim \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}1 & - . 4 & - . 6 & 0 \\ 0 & . 66 & - . 56 & 0 \\ 0 & - . 66 & . 56 & 0\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} sim \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}1 & - . 4 & - . 6 & 0 \\ 0 & . 66 & - . 56 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} & sim \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}1 & - . 4 & - . 6 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & - . 85 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} sim \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}1 & 0 & - . 94 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & - . 85 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix}$$ The general solution is $$p_{ \text{C} } = .94p_{ \text{S} }$$ , $$p_{ \text{E} } = .85p_{ \text{S} }$$ , and $$p_{ \text{S} }$$ is free. The equilibrium price vector for the economy has the form $$\mathbf{p} = \begin{bmatrix} p_{ \text{C} } \\ p_{ \text{E} } \\ p_{ \text{S} } \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} .94 p_{ \text{S} } \\ .85 p_{ \text{S} } \\ p_{ \text{S} } \end{bmatrix} = p_{ \text{S} } \begin{bmatrix} .94 \\ .85 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$$ Any (nonnegative) choice for $$p_{ \text{S} }$$ results in a choice of equilibrium prices. For instance, if we take $$p_{ \text{S} }$$ to be $$100$$ (or $$\$100 \text{million}$$ ), then $$p_{ \text{C} } = 94$$ and $$p_{ \text{E} } = 85$$ . The incomes and expenditures of each sector will be equal if the output of Coal is priced at $$\$94 \text{million}$$ , that of Electric at $$\$85 \text{million}$$ , and that of Steel at $$\$100 \text{million}$$ .

title: Example 2
snippet: Example 2: Example 2 The network in Figure 2 shows the traffic flow (in vehicles per hour) over several one-way streets in downtown Baltimore during a typical early afternoon. Determine the general flow pattern for the network. Solution...
body_xml: Example 2 The network in Figure 2 shows the traffic flow (in vehicles per hour) over several one-way streets in downtown Baltimore during a typical early afternoon. Determine the general flow pattern for the network. Solution Write equations that describe the flow, and then find the general solution of the system. Label the street intersections (junctions) and the unknown flows in the branches, as shown in Figure 2. At each intersection, set the flow in equal to the flow out. Also, the total flow into the network $$(500 + 300 + 100 + 400)$$ equals the total flow out of the network $$(300 + x_{3} + 600)$$ , which simplifies to $$x_{3} = 400$$ . Combine this equation with a rearrangement of the first four equations to obtain the following system of equations: $$x_{1} & + & x_{2} & & & & & & & = & 800 & & x_{2} & - & x_{3} & + & x_{4} & & & = & 300 & & & & & & x_{4} & + & x_{5} & = & 500 x_{1} & & & & & & & + & x_{5} & = & 600 & & & & x_{3} & & & & & = & 400$$ Row reduction of the associated augmented matrix leads to $$x_{1} & & & & & & & + & x_{5} & = & 600 & & x_{2} & & & & & - & x_{5} & = & 200 & & & & x_{3} & & & & & = & 400 & & & & & & x_{4} & + & x_{5} & = & 500$$ The general flow pattern for the network is described by $$\left{\right. \begin{matrix}x_{1} = 600 - x_{5} \\ x_{2} = 200 + x_{5} \\ x_{3} = 400 \\ x_{4} = 500 - x_{5} \\ x_{5} \text{is} \text{free} \end{matrix}$$ A negative flow in a network branch corresponds to flow in the direction opposite to that shown on the model. Since the streets in this problem are one way, none of the variables here can be negative. This fact leads to certain limitations on the possible values of the variables. For instance, $$x_{5} \leq 500$$ because $$x_{4}$$ cannot be negative. Other constraints on the variables are considered in Practice Problem 2.

body_xml:
<note type="definition" source_type="definition" title="Definition">
    <heading level="2">Definition</heading>
    <paragraph>An indexed set of vectors $$\left\{ \mathbf{v}_{1},\left. \text{…} ,\mathbf{v}_{\mathbf{p}} \right\} \right.$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ is said to be linearly independent if the vector equation</paragraph>
    <paragraph>$$x_{1} \mathbf{v}_{1} + x_{2} \mathbf{v}_{2} + \hdots + x_{p} \mathbf{v}_{p} = 0$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>has only the trivial solution. The set $$\left\{ \mathbf{v}_{1},\left. \text{…} ,\mathbf{v}_{\mathbf{p}} \right\} \right.$$ is said to be linearly dependent if there exist weights $${c_{1},} \text{…} ,c_{p}$$ , not all zero, such that</paragraph>
    <paragraph>(2)</paragraph>
    <paragraph>$$c_{1} \mathbf{v}_{1} + c_{2} \mathbf{v}_{2} + \hdots + c_{p} \mathbf{v}_{p} = 0$$</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Example 1
snippet: Example 1: Example 1 Let \mathbf{v}_{1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix} , \mathbf{v}_{2} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ 5 \\ 6 \end{bmatrix}, and \mathbf{v}_{3} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} . Determine if the set...
body_xml:
<example number="1">
    <heading level="2">Example 1</heading>
    <paragraph>Let $$\mathbf{v}_{1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix} ,$$ $$\mathbf{v}_{2} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ 5 \\ 6 \end{bmatrix},$$ and $$\mathbf{v}_{3} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} .$$</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>Determine if the set $$\{\mathbf{v}_{1} \text{,} \mathbf{v}_{2} \text{,} \mathbf{v}_{3}\}$$ is linearly independent.</item>
      <item>If possible, find a linear dependence relation among $$\mathbf{v}_{1}$$ , $$\mathbf{v}_{2}$$ , and $$\mathbf{v}_{3}$$ .</item>
    </list>
    <heading level="3">Solution</heading>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>We must determine if there is a nontrivial solution of equation (1) above. Row operations on the associated augmented matrix show that $$\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 4 & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & 5 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 6 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \sim \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 4 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & - 3 & - 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$$</item>
    </list>
    <list type="unordered">
      <item>Clearly, $$x_{1}$$ and $$x_{2}$$ are basic variables, and $$x_{3}$$ is free. Each nonzero value of $$x_{3}$$ determines a nontrivial solution of (1). Hence $$\mathbf{v}_{1},\mathbf{v}_{2},\mathbf{v}_{3}$$ are linearly dependent (and not linearly independent).</item>
    </list>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>To find a linear dependence relation among $$\mathbf{v}_{1}$$ , $$\mathbf{v}_{2}$$ , and $$\mathbf{v}_{3}$$ , completely row reduce the augmented matrix and write the new system: $$\begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}1 & 0 & - 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} & \begin{matrix}x_{1} & & - & 2 x_{3} & = & 0 \\ & x_{2} & + & x_{3} & = & 0 \\ & & & 0 & = & 0\end{matrix}$$ Thus $$x_{1} = 2x_{3}$$ , $$x_{2} = - x_{3}$$ , and $$x_{3}$$ is free. Choose any nonzero value for $$x_{3}$$ —say, $$x_{3} = 5$$ . Then $$x_{1} = 10$$ and $$x_{2} = - 5$$ . Substitute these values into equation (1) and obtain $$10 \mathbf{v}_{1} - 5 \mathbf{v}_{2} + 5 \mathbf{v}_{3} = 0$$ This is one (out of infinitely many) possible linear dependence relations among $$\mathbf{v}_{1}$$ , $$\mathbf{v}_{2}$$ , and $$\mathbf{v}_{3}$$ .</item>
    </list>
  </example>

<example number="2">
    <heading level="2">Example 2</heading>
    <paragraph>Determine if the columns of the matrix $$A = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 & 4 \\ 1 & 2 & {- 1} \\ 5 & 8 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$$ are linearly independent.</paragraph>
    <heading level="3">Solution</heading>
    <paragraph>To study $$A\mathbf{x} = 0$$ , row reduce the augmented matrix:</paragraph>
    <paragraph>$$\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 & 4 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & - 1 & 0 \\ 5 & 8 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} ∼ \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & - 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & - 2 & 5 & 0 \end{bmatrix} ∼ \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & - 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 3 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>At this point, it is clear that there are three basic variables and no free variables. So the equation $$A\mathbf{x} = 0$$ has only the trivial solution, and the columns of $$A$$ are linearly independent.</paragraph>

title: Example 3
snippet: Example 3: Example 3 Determine if the following sets of vectors are linearly independent. \mathbf{v}_{1} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} , \mathbf{v}_{2} = \begin{bmatrix} 6 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} \mathbf{v}_{1} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 2...
body_xml:
<example number="3">
    <heading level="2">Example 3</heading>
    <paragraph>Determine if the following sets of vectors are linearly independent.</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>$$\mathbf{v}_{1} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} , \mathbf{v}_{2} = \begin{bmatrix} 6 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}$$</item>
      <item>$$\mathbf{v}_{1} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} , \mathbf{v}_{2} = \begin{bmatrix} 6 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}$$</item>
    </list>
    <heading level="3">Solution</heading>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>Notice that $$\mathbf{v}_{2}$$ is a multiple of $$\mathbf{v}_{1}$$ , namely $$\mathbf{v}_{2} = 2\mathbf{v}_{1}$$ . Hence $$- 2\mathbf{v}_{1} + \mathbf{v}_{2} = 0$$ , which shows that $$\{\mathbf{v}_{1} \text{,} \mathbf{v}_{2}\}$$ is linearly dependent.</item>
      <item>The vectors $$\mathbf{v}_{1}$$ and $$\mathbf{v}_{2}$$ are certainly not multiples of one another. Could they be linearly dependent? Suppose $$c$$ and $$d$$ satisfy $$c \mathbf{v}_{1} + d \mathbf{v}_{2} = 0$$ If $$c \neq 0$$ , then we can solve for $$\mathbf{v}_{1}$$ in terms of $$\mathbf{v}_{2}$$ , namely $$\mathbf{v}_{1} = ( - d/c)\mathbf{v}_{2}$$ . This result is impossible because $$\mathbf{v}_{1}$$ is not a multiple of $$\mathbf{v}_{2}$$ . So $$c$$ must be zero. Similarly, $$d$$ must also be zero. Thus $$\{\mathbf{v}_{1} \text{,} \mathbf{v}_{2}\}$$ is a linearly independent set.</item>
    </list>
  </example>

    <paragraph>A set of two vectors $$\{\mathbf{v}_{1} \text{,} \mathbf{v}_{2}\}$$ is linearly dependent if at least one of the vectors is a multiple of the other. The set is linearly independent if and only if neither of the vectors is a multiple of the other.</paragraph>

title: Theorem 7
snippet: Theorem 7: Theorem 7 Characterization of Linearly Dependent Sets An indexed set S = \{\mathbf{v}_{1}, \text{…} ,\mathbf{v}_{p}\} of two or more vectors is linearly dependent if and only if at least one of the vectors in S is a linear...
body_xml:
<note type="procedure" source_type="procedure" title="Theorem 7">
    <heading level="2">Theorem 7</heading>
    <heading level="3">Characterization of Linearly Dependent Sets</heading>
    <paragraph>An indexed set $$S = \{\mathbf{v}_{1}, \text{…} ,\mathbf{v}_{p}\}$$ of two or more vectors is linearly dependent if and only if at least one of the vectors in $$S$$ is a linear combination of the others. In fact, if $$S$$ is linearly dependent and $$\mathbf{v}_{1} \neq 0$$ , then some $$\mathbf{v}_{j}$$ (with $$j > 1$$ ) is a linear combination of the preceding vectors, $$\mathbf{v}_{1} \text{,…,} \mathbf{v}_{j - 1}$$ .</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Example 4
snippet: Example 4: Example 4 Let \mathbf{u} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} and \mathbf{v} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 6 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} . Describe the set spanned by \mathbf{u} and \mathbf{v} , and explain why a vector \mathbf{w} is in...
body_xml: Example 4 Let $$\mathbf{u} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}$$ and $$\mathbf{v} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 6 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}$$ . Describe the set spanned by $$\mathbf{u}$$ and $$\mathbf{v}$$ , and explain why a vector $$\mathbf{w}$$ is in $$\text{Span} \{\mathbf{u} \text{,} \mathbf{v}\}$$ if and only if $$\{\mathbf{u} \text{,} \mathbf{v} \text{,} \mathbf{w}\}$$ is linearly dependent. Solution The vectors $$\mathbf{u}$$ and $$\mathbf{v}$$ are linearly independent because neither vector is a multiple of the other, and so they span a plane in $$\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ . (See Section 1.3.) In fact, $$\text{Span\{} \mathbf{u} \text{,} \mathbf{v} \text{\}}$$ is the $$x_{1}x_{2} \text{-plane}$$ (with $$x_{3} = 0)$$ . If $$\mathbf{w}$$ is a linear combination of $$\mathbf{u}$$ and $$\mathbf{v}$$ , then $$\{\mathbf{u} \text{,} \mathbf{v} \text{,} \mathbf{w}\}$$ is linearly dependent, by transformation (or function or mapping). Conversely, suppose that $$\{\mathbf{u} \text{,} \mathbf{v} \text{,} \mathbf{w}\}$$ is linearly dependent. by Theorem 7, some vector in $$\{\mathbf{u} \text{,} \mathbf{v} \text{,} \mathbf{w}\}$$ is a linear combination of the preceding vectors (since $$\mathbf{u} \neq 0)$$ . That vector must be $$\mathbf{w}$$ , since $$\mathbf{v}$$ is not a multiple of $$\mathbf{u}$$ . So $$\mathbf{w}$$ is in $$\text{Span\{} \mathbf{u} \text{,} \mathbf{v} \text{\}}$$ . See Figure 2. snippet: Theorem 8: Theorem 8 If a set contains more vectors than there are entries in each vector, then the set is linearly dependent. That is, any set \text{\{} \mathbf{v}_{1}, \text{…} ,\mathbf{v}_{p} \text{\}} in \mathbb{R}^{n} is linearly...

<note type="procedure" source_type="procedure" title="Theorem 8">
    <heading level="2">Theorem 8</heading>
    <paragraph>If a set contains more vectors than there are entries in each vector, then the set is linearly dependent. That is, any set $$\text{\{} \mathbf{v}_{1}, \text{…} ,\mathbf{v}_{p} \text{\}}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ is linearly dependent if $$p > n$$ .</paragraph>
  </note>

<example number="6">
    <heading level="2">Example 6</heading>
    <paragraph>Determine by inspection if the given set is linearly dependent.</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>$$\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 7 \\ 6 \end{bmatrix} , \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 0 \\ 9 \end{bmatrix} , \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 1 \\ 5 \end{bmatrix} , \begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ 1 \\ 8 \end{bmatrix}$$</item>
      <item>$$\begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 3 \\ 5 \end{bmatrix} , \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} , \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 8 \end{bmatrix}$$</item>
      <item>$$\begin{bmatrix} - 2 \\ 4 \\ 6 \\ 10 \end{bmatrix} , \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ - 6 \\ - 9 \\ 15 \end{bmatrix}$$</item>
    </list>
    <heading level="3">Solution</heading>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>The set contains four vectors, each of which has only three entries. So the set is linearly dependent by Theorem 8.</item>
      <item>Theorem 8 does not apply here because the number of vectors does not exceed the number of entries in each vector. Since the zero vector is in the set, the set is linearly dependent by Theorem 9.</item>
      <item>Compare the corresponding entries of the two vectors. The second vector seems to be $$- 3/2$$ times the first vector. This relation holds for the first three pairs of entries, but fails for the fourth pair. Thus neither of the vectors is a multiple of the other, and hence they are linearly independent.</item>
    </list>
  </example>

title: Example 1
snippet: Example 1: Example 1 Let A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & {- 3} \\ 3 & 5 \\ {- 1} & 7 \end{bmatrix} , \mathbf{u} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 2 \\ {- 1} \end{array} \right\rbrack , \mathbf{b} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 3 \\ 2 \\ {- 5}...
body_xml: Example 1 Let $$A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & {- 3} \\ 3 & 5 \\ {- 1} & 7 \end{bmatrix}$$ , $$\mathbf{u} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 2 \\ {- 1} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , $$\mathbf{b} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 3 \\ 2 \\ {- 5} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , $$\mathbf{c} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 2 \\ 5 \end{bmatrix}$$ , and define a transformation $$T:\mathbb{R}^{2}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ by $$T(\mathbf{x}) = A\mathbf{x}$$ , so that $$T ( \mathbf{x} ) = A \mathbf{x} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & - 3 \\ 3 & 5 \\ - 1 & 7 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x_{1} \\ x_{2} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} x_{1} - 3 x_{2} \\ 3 x_{1} + 5 x_{2} \\ - x_{1} + 7 x_{2} \end{bmatrix}$$ Find $$T(\mathbf{u})$$ , the image of $$\mathbf{u}$$ under the transformation $$T$$ . Find an $$\mathbf{x}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{2}$$ whose image under $$T$$ is $$\mathbf{b}$$ . Is there more than one $$\mathbf{x}$$ whose image under $$T$$ is $$\mathbf{b} ?$$ Determine if $$\mathbf{c}$$ is in the range of the transformation $$T$$ . Solution Compute $$T ( \mathbf{u} ) = A \mathbf{u} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & - 3 \\ 3 & 5 \\ - 1 & 7 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ - 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ 1 \\ - 9 \end{bmatrix}$$ Solve $$T(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{b}$$ for $$\mathbf{x}$$ . That is, solve $$A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$$ , or (1) $$\begin{bmatrix} 1 & - 3 \\ 3 & 5 \\ - 1 & 7 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x_{1} \\ x_{2} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 2 \\ - 5 \end{bmatrix}$$ Using the method discussed in Section 1.4, row reduce the augmented matrix: (2) $$\begin{bmatrix} 1 & - 3 & 3 \\ 3 & 5 & 2 \\ - 1 & 7 & - 5 \end{bmatrix} \sim \begin{bmatrix} 1 & - 3 & 3 \\ 0 & 14 & - 7 \\ 0 & 4 & - 2 \end{bmatrix} \sim \begin{bmatrix} 1 & - 3 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & - . 5 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \sim \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 1.5 \\ 0 & 1 & - . 5 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$$ Hence $$x_{1} = 1.5$$ , $$x_{2} = - .5$$ , and $$\mathbf{x} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 1.5 \\ {- .5} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ . The image of this $$\mathbf{x}$$ under $$T$$ is the given vector $$\mathbf{b}$$ . Any $$\mathbf{x}$$ whose image under $$T$$ is $$\mathbf{b}$$ must satisfy equation (1). From (2), it is clear that equation (1) has a unique solution. So there is exactly one $$\mathbf{x}$$ whose image is $$\mathbf{b}$$ . The vector $$\mathbf{c}$$ is in the range of $$T$$ if $$\mathbf{c}$$ is the image of some $$\mathbf{x}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{2}$$ , that is, if $$\mathbf{c} = T(\mathbf{x})$$ for some $$\mathbf{x}$$ . This is just another way of asking if the system $$A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{c}$$ is consistent. To find the answer, row reduce the augmented matrix: $$\begin{bmatrix} 1 & - 3 & 3 \\ 3 & 5 & 2 \\ - 1 & 7 & 5 \end{bmatrix} \sim \begin{bmatrix} 1 & - 3 & 3 \\ 0 & 14 & - 7 \\ 0 & 4 & 8 \end{bmatrix} \sim \begin{bmatrix} 1 & - 3 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 14 & - 7 \end{bmatrix} \sim \begin{bmatrix} 1 & - 3 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & - 35 \end{bmatrix}$$ The third equation, $$0 = - 35$$ , shows that the system is inconsistent. So $$\mathbf{c}$$ is not in the range of $$T$$ .

title: Example 3
snippet: Example 3: Example 3 Let A = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{rr} 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 \end{array} \right\rbrack . The transformation \mathbf{T}:\mathbb{R}^{ \text{2} }\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{2} defined by T(\mathbf{x}) = A\mathbf{x} is called a shear...
body_xml: Example 3 Let $$A = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{rr} 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ . The transformation $$\mathbf{T}:\mathbb{R}^{ \text{2} }\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{2}$$ defined by $$T(\mathbf{x}) = A\mathbf{x}$$ is called a shear transformation. It can be shown that if $$T$$ acts on each point in the $$2 \times 2$$ square shown in Figure 4, then the set of images forms the sheared parallelogram. The key idea is to show that $$T$$ maps line segments onto line segments (as shown in Exercise 35) and then to check that the corners of the square map onto the vertices of the parallelogram. For instance, the image of the point $$\mathbf{u} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 0 \\ 2 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ is $$T(\mathbf{u}) = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{rr} 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 \end{array} \right\rbrack\left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 0 \\ 2 \end{array} \right\rbrack = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 4 \\ 2 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , and the image of $$\left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 2 \\ 2 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ is $$\left\lbrack \begin{array}{rr} 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 \end{array} \right\rbrack\left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 2 \\ 2 \end{array} \right\rbrack = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 6 \\ 2 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ . $$T$$ deforms the square as if the top of the square were pushed to the right while the base is held fixed. Shear transformations appear in physics, geology, and crystallography. Click here for an Interactive version of Figure 4

body_xml:
<note type="definition" source_type="definition" title="Definition">
    <heading level="2">Definition</heading>
    <paragraph>A transformation (or mapping) $$T$$ is linear if</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>$$T(\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v}) = T(\mathbf{u}) + T(\mathbf{v})$$ for all $$\mathbf{u} \text{,} \mathbf{v}$$ in the domain of $$T$$ ;</item>
      <item>$$T(c\mathbf{u}) = cT(\mathbf{u})$$ for all scalars $$c$$ and all $$\mathbf{u}$$ in the domain of $$T$$ .</item>
    </list>
  </note>

snippet: Example 4: Example 4 Given a scalar r , define T:\mathbb{R}^{2}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{2} by T(\mathbf{x}) = r\mathbf{x} . T is called a contraction when 0 \leq r \leq 1 and a dilation when r > 1 . Let r = 3 , and show that T is a linear...
body_xml: Example 4 Given a scalar $$r$$ , define $$T:\mathbb{R}^{2}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{2}$$ by $$T(\mathbf{x}) = r\mathbf{x}$$ . $$T$$ is called a contraction when $$0 \leq r \leq 1$$ and a dilation when $$r > 1$$ . Let $$r = 3$$ , and show that $$T$$ is a linear transformation. Solution Let $$\mathbf{u}$$ , $$\mathbf{v}$$ be in $$\mathbb{R}^{2}$$ and let $$c$$ , $$d$$ be scalars. Then $$T \left(\right. c \mathbf{u} + d \mathbf{v} \left.\right) & = 3 \left(\right. c \mathbf{u} + d \mathbf{v} \left.\right) & \text{Definition} \text{of} T & \begin{matrix}= 3 c \mathbf{u} + 3 d \mathbf{v} \\ = c \left(\right. 3 \mathbf{u} \left.\right) + d \left(\right. 3 \mathbf{v} \left.\right)\end{matrix} \left.\right} & \text{Vector} \text{arithmetic} & = c T \left(\right. \mathbf{u} \left.\right) + d T \left(\right. \mathbf{v} \left.\right) &$$ Thus $$T$$ is a linear transformation because it satisfies (4). See Figure 5. Click here to see an interactive example of dilation and contraction

title: Example 5
snippet: Example 5: Example 5 Define a linear transformation T:\mathbb{R}^{2}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{2} by T ( \mathbf{x} ) = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & - 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x_{1} \\ x_{2} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} - x_{2} \\...
body_xml: Example 5 Define a linear transformation $$T:\mathbb{R}^{2}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{2}$$ by $$T ( \mathbf{x} ) = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & - 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x_{1} \\ x_{2} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} - x_{2} \\ x_{1} \end{bmatrix}$$ Find the images under $$T$$ of $$\mathbf{u} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$$ , $$\mathbf{v} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}$$ , and $$\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v} = \begin{bmatrix} 6 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix}$$ . Solution $$T \left(\right. \mathbf{u} \left.\right) = \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}0 & - 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}4 \\ 1\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}- 1 \\ 4\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} , T \left(\right. \mathbf{v} \left.\right) = \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}0 & - 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}2 \\ 3\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}- 3 \\ 2\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} , T \left(\right. \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v} \left.\right) = \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}0 & - 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}6 \\ 4\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}- 4 \\ 6\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix}$$ Note that $$T(\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v})$$ is obviously equal to $$T(\mathbf{u}) + T(\mathbf{v})$$ . It appears from Figure 6 that $$T$$ rotates $$\mathbf{u}$$ , $$\mathbf{v}$$ , and $$\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v}$$ counterclockwise about the origin through $$90{^\circ}$$ . In fact, $$T$$ transforms the entire parallelogram determined by $$\mathbf{u}$$ and $$\mathbf{v}$$ into the one determined by $$T(\mathbf{u})$$ and $$T(\mathbf{v})$$ . (See Exercise 36.) Click here for an interactive example of the properties of linear transformations

title: Example 6
snippet: Example 6: Example 6 A company manufactures two products, \text{B} and \text{C} . Using data from Example 7 in Section 1.3, we construct a “unit cost” matrix, U = \lbrack\mathbf{b} \mathbf{c}\rbrack , whose columns describe the “costs per...
body_xml:
<example number="6">
    <heading level="2">Example 6</heading>
    <paragraph>A company manufactures two products, $$\text{B}$$ and $$\text{C}$$ . Using data from Example 7 in Section 1.3, we construct a “unit cost” matrix, $$U = \lbrack\mathbf{b} \mathbf{c}\rbrack$$ , whose columns describe the “costs per dollar of output” for the products:</paragraph>
    <paragraph>$$\text{Product} \begin{matrix} \text{B} & \text{C} \end{matrix} U = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}.45 & .40 \\ .25 & .30 \\ .15 & .15\end{matrix} \left]\right. \begin{matrix} \text{Materials} \\ \text{Labor} \\ \text{Overhead} \end{matrix}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Let $$\mathbf{x} = \left( x_{1} \text{,} x_{2} \right)$$ be a “production” vector, corresponding to $$x_{1}$$ dollars of product $$\text{B}$$ and $$x_{2}$$ dollars of product $$\text{C}$$ , and define $$T:\mathbb{R}^{2}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ by</paragraph>
    <paragraph>$$T \left(\right. \mathbf{x} \left.\right) = U \mathbf{x} = x_{1} \left[\right. .45 .25 .15 \left]\right. + x_{2} \left[\right. .40 .30 .15 \left]\right. = \left[\right. \text{Total cost of materials} \text{Total cost of labor} \text{Total cost of overhead} \left]\right.$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>The mapping $$T$$ transforms a list of production quantities (measured in dollars) into a list of total costs. The linearity of this mapping is reflected in two ways:</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>If production is increased by a factor of, say, $$4$$ , from $$\mathbf{x}$$ to $$4\mathbf{x}$$ , then the costs will increase by the same factor, from $$T(\mathbf{x})$$ to $$4T(\mathbf{x})$$ .</item>
      <item>If $$\mathbf{x}$$ and $$\mathbf{y}$$ are production vectors, then the total cost vector associated with the combined production $$\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{y}$$ is precisely the sum of the cost vectors $$T(\mathbf{x})$$ and $$T(\mathbf{y})$$ .</item>
    </list>
  </example>

body_xml: Example 1 The columns of $$I_{2} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$$ are $$\mathbf{e}_{1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}$$ and $$\mathbf{e}_{2} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$$ . Suppose $$T$$ is a linear transformation from $$\mathbb{R}^{2}$$ into $$\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ such that $$T ( \mathbf{e}_{1} ) = \begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ - 7 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} \text{and} T ( \mathbf{e}_{2} ) = \begin{bmatrix} - 3 \\ 8 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}$$ With no additional information, find a formula for the image of an arbitrary $$\mathbf{x}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{2}$$ . Solution Write (1) $$\mathbf{x} = \begin{bmatrix} x_{1} \\ x_{2} \end{bmatrix} = x_{1} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} + x_{2} \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = x_{1} \mathbf{e}_{1} + x_{2} \mathbf{e}_{2}$$ Since $$T$$ is a linear transformation, (2) $$T \left(\right. \mathbf{x} \left.\right) & = & x_{1} T \left(\right. \mathbf{e}_{1} \left.\right) + x_{2} T \left(\right. \mathbf{e}_{2} \left.\right) & = & x_{1} \left[\right. \begin{matrix}5 \\ - 7 \\ 2\end{matrix} \left]\right. + x_{2} \left[\right. \begin{matrix}- 3 \\ 8 \\ 0\end{matrix} \left]\right. = \left[\right. \begin{matrix} 5 x_{1} - 3 x_{2} \\ - 7 x_{1} + 8 x_{2} \\ 2 x_{1} + 0\end{matrix} \left]\right.$$

snippet: Theorem 10: Theorem 10 Let T:\mathbb{R}^{n}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{m} be a linear transformation. Then there exists a unique matrix A such that T ( \mathbf{x} ) = A ( \mathbf{x} ) \text{for} \text{all} \mathbf{x} \text{in} \textbf{R}^{n} In...
body_xml:
<note type="procedure" source_type="procedure" title="Theorem 10">
    <heading level="2">Theorem 10</heading>
    <paragraph>Let $$T:\mathbb{R}^{n}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{m}$$ be a linear transformation. Then there exists a unique matrix $$A$$ such that</paragraph>
    <paragraph>$$T ( \mathbf{x} ) = A ( \mathbf{x} ) \text{for} \text{all} \mathbf{x} \text{in} \textbf{R}^{n}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>In fact, $$A$$ is the $$m \times n$$ matrix whose $$j \text{th}$$ column is the vector $$T(\mathbf{e}_{j})$$ , where $$\mathbf{e}_{j}$$ is the $$j \text{th}$$ column of the identity matrix in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ :</paragraph>
    <paragraph>(3)</paragraph>
    <paragraph>$$A = \begin{bmatrix} T \left(\right. \mathbf{e}_{1} \left.\right) & \hdots & T \left(\right. \mathbf{e}_{n} \left.\right) \end{bmatrix}$$</paragraph>
  </note>

body_xml: Example 3 Let $$T:\mathbb{R}^{2}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{2}$$ be the transformation that rotates each point in $$\mathbb{R}^{2}$$ about the origin through an angle $$\varphi$$ , with counterclockwise rotation for a positive angle. We could show geometrically that such a transformation is linear. (See Figure 6 in Section 1.8.) Find the standard matrix $$A$$ of this transformation. Solution $$\left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 1 \\ 0 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ rotates into $$\left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} {\cos\varphi} \\ {\sin\varphi} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , and $$\left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 0 \\ 1 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ rotates into $$\left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} {- \sin\varphi} \\ {\cos\varphi} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ . See Figure 1. By Theorem 10, $$A = \begin{bmatrix} cos \varphi & - sin \varphi \\ sin \varphi & cos \varphi \end{bmatrix}$$ Click here for an interactive version of Figure 1 Example 5 in Section 1.8 is a special case of this transformation, with $$\varphi = \pi/2$$ .

title: Example 4
snippet: Example 4: Example 4 Let T be the linear transformation whose standard matrix is A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & - 4 & 8 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & - 1 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 5 \end{bmatrix} Does T map \mathbb{R}^{4} onto \mathbb{R}^{3} \text{?} Is T a one-to-one...
body_xml:
<example number="4">
    <heading level="2">Example 4</heading>
    <paragraph>Let $$T$$ be the linear transformation whose standard matrix is</paragraph>
    <paragraph>$$A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & - 4 & 8 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & - 1 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 5 \end{bmatrix}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Does $$T$$ map $$\mathbb{R}^{4}$$ onto $$\mathbb{R}^{3} \text{?}$$ Is $$T$$ a one-to-one mapping?</paragraph>
    <heading level="3">Solution</heading>
    <paragraph>Since $$A$$ happens to be in echelon form, we can see at once that $$A$$ has a pivot position in each row. By Theorem 4 in Section 1.4, for each $$\mathbf{b}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ , the equation $$A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$$ is consistent. In other words, the linear transformation $$T$$ maps $$\mathbb{R}^{4}$$ (its domain) onto $$\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ . However, since the equation $$A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$$ has a free variable (because there are four variables and only three basic variables), each $$\mathbf{b}$$ is the image of more than one $$\mathbf{x}$$ . That is, $$T$$ is not one-to-one.</paragraph>
  </example>

snippet: Theorem 12: Theorem 12 Let T:\mathbb{R}^{n}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{m} be a linear transformation, and let A be the standard matrix for T . Then: T maps \mathbb{R}^{n} onto \mathbb{R}^{m} if and only if the columns of A span \mathbb{R}^{m} ;...

    <heading level="2">Theorem 12</heading>
    <paragraph>Let $$T:\mathbb{R}^{n}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{m}$$ be a linear transformation, and let $$A$$ be the standard matrix for $$T$$ . Then:</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>$$T$$ maps $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ onto $$\mathbb{R}^{m}$$ if and only if the columns of $$A$$ span $$\mathbb{R}^{m}$$ ;</item>
      <item>$$T$$ is one-to-one if and only if the columns of $$A$$ are linearly independent.</item>
    </list>
  </note>
