title: Example 3
snippet: Example 3: Example 3 Use the results of Examples 1 and 2 to construct a singular value decomposition of A = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{rrr} 4 & 11 & 14 \\ 8 & 7 & {- 2} \end{array} \right\rbrack . Solution A construction can be divided...
body_xml:
<example number="3">
    <heading level="2">Example 3</heading>
    <paragraph>Use the results of Examples 1 and 2 to construct a singular value decomposition of $$A = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{rrr} 4 & 11 & 14 \\ 8 & 7 & {- 2} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ .</paragraph>
    <heading level="3">Solution</heading>
    <paragraph>A construction can be divided into three steps.</paragraph>
    <note type="margin_note" source_type="margin_note">
      <paragraph>STUDY GUIDE offers additional resources for learning to compute an SVD.</paragraph>
    </note>
    <paragraph>Step 1. Find an orthogonal diagonalization of ﻿ $$\textit{\textbf{A}}^{\mathbf{T}}\textit{\textbf{A}}$$ That is, find the eigenvalues of ﻿ $$\textit{A}^{T}\textit{A}$$ and a corresponding orthonormal set of eigenvectors. If $$A$$ ﻿had only two columns, the calculations could be done by hand. Larger matrices usually require a matrix program. However, for the matrix $$A$$ here, the eigendata for $$A^{T} A$$ ﻿are provided in Example 1﻿.</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Step 2. Set up $$\mathbf{\mathit{V}}$$ and ﻿ $$\Sigma$$ . Arrange the eigenvalues of ﻿ $$A^{T} A$$ in decreasing order. In Example 1, the eigenvalues are already listed in decreasing order: $$360$$ , $$90$$ , and $$0$$ . The corresponding unit eigenvectors, $$\mathbf{v}_{1}$$ ﻿, $$\mathbf{v}_{2}$$ ﻿, and $$\mathbf{v}_{3}$$ ﻿, are the right singular vectors of $$A$$ ﻿. Using Example 1, construct</paragraph>
    <paragraph>$$V = \left[\textbf{v}_{1} \textbf{v}_{2} \textbf{v}_{3}\right] = \begin{bmatrix} 1 / 3 & - 2 / 3 & 2 / 3 \\ 2 / 3 & - 1 / 3 & - 2 / 3 \\ 2 / 3 & 2 / 3 & 1 / 3 \end{bmatrix}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>The square roots of the eigenvalues are the singular values:</paragraph>
    <paragraph>$$\sigma_{1} = 6 \sqrt{10} , \sigma_{2} = 3 \sqrt{10} , \sigma_{3} = 0$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>The nonzero singular values are the diagonal entries of $$D$$ . The matrix $$\text{Σ}$$ is the same size as $$A$$ , with $$D$$ in its upper left corner and with $$0$$ ’s elsewhere.</paragraph>
    <paragraph>$$D = \left[\right. 6 \sqrt{10} & 0 0 & 3 \sqrt{10} \left]\right. , \Sigma = \left[\right. D & 0 \left]\right. = \left[\right. 6 \sqrt{10} & 0 & 0 0 & 3 \sqrt{10} & 0 \left]\right.$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Step 3. Construct $$\mathbf{U}$$ . When ﻿ $$A$$ has rank ﻿ $$r$$ , the first $$r$$ columns of ﻿ $$U$$ are the normalized vectors obtained from $$A\textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,A\textbf{v}_{r}$$ . In this example, $$A$$ has two nonzero singular values, so $$\text{rank} A = 2$$ . Recall from equation (2) and the paragraph before Example 2 that $$\text{∥} \textit{A}\textbf{v}_{1} \text{∥} = \sigma_{1}$$ and $$\text{∥} \textit{A}\textbf{v}_{2} \text{∥} = \sigma_{2}$$ . Thus</paragraph>
    <paragraph>$$\mathbf{u}_{1} & = & \frac{1}{\sigma_{1}} A \mathbf{v}_{1} & = & \frac{1}{6 \sqrt{10}} \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}18 \\ 6\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} & = & \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}3 / \sqrt{10} \\ 1 / \sqrt{10}\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} \mathbf{u}_{2} & = & \frac{1}{\sigma_{2}} A \mathbf{v}_{2} & = & \frac{1}{3 \sqrt{10}} \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}3 \\ - 9\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} & = & \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}1 / \sqrt{10} \\ - 3 / \sqrt{10}\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Note that $$\left\{ \textbf{u}_{1},\textbf{u}_{2} \right\}$$ ﻿ is already a basis for ﻿ $$\mathbb{R}^{2}$$ . Thus no additional vectors are needed for $$U$$ , and $$U = \left\lbrack \textbf{u}_{1} \textbf{u}_{2} \right\rbrack$$ . The singular value decomposition of ﻿ $$A$$ is</paragraph>
    <paragraph>$$\begin{matrix}A & = & \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}3 / \sqrt{10} & 1 / \sqrt{10} \\ 1 / \sqrt{10} & - 3 / \sqrt{10}\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} & \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}6 \sqrt{10} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 \sqrt{10} & 0\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} & \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}1 / 3 & 2 / 3 & 2 / 3 \\ - 2 / 3 & - 1 / 3 & 2 / 3 \\ 2 / 3 & - 2 / 3 & 1 / 3\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} \\ & & \uparrow & \uparrow & \uparrow \\ & & U & \Sigma & V^{T}\end{matrix}$$</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Example 4
snippet: Example 4: Example 4 Find a singular value decomposition of A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & - 1 \\ - 2 & 2 \\ 2 & - 2 \end{bmatrix} . Solution First, compute A^{T}A = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{rr} 9 & {- 9} \\ {- 9} & 9 \end{array} \right\rbrack...
body_xml: Example 4 Find a singular value decomposition of $$A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & - 1 \\ - 2 & 2 \\ 2 & - 2 \end{bmatrix} .$$ Solution First, compute $$A^{T}A = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{rr} 9 & {- 9} \\ {- 9} & 9 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ . The eigenvalues of $$A^{T}A$$ are $$18$$ and $$0$$ , with corresponding unit eigenvectors $$\textbf{v}_{1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 / \sqrt{2} \\ - 1 / \sqrt{2} \end{bmatrix} , \textbf{v}_{2} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 / \sqrt{2} \\ 1 / \sqrt{2} \end{bmatrix}$$ These unit vectors form the columns of $$V$$ : $$V = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}\textbf{v}_{1} & \textbf{v}_{2}\end{matrix} \left]\right. = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}1 \sqrt{2} & 1 \sqrt{2} \\ - 1 \sqrt{2} & 1 \sqrt{2}\end{matrix} \left]\right.$$ The singular values are $$\sigma_{1} = \sqrt{18} = 3\sqrt{2}$$ and $$\sigma_{2} = 0$$ . Since there is only one nonzero singular value, the “matrix” $$D$$ may be written as a single number. That is, $$D = 3\sqrt{2}$$ . The matrix $$\text{Σ}$$ is the same size as $$A$$ , with $$D$$ in its upper left corner: $$\Sigma = \left[\right. D & 0 0 & 0 0 & 0 \left]\right. = \left[\right. 3 \sqrt{2} & 0 0 & 0 0 & 0 \left]\right.$$ To construct $$U$$ , first construct $$A\textbf{v}_{1}$$ and $$A\textbf{v}_{2}$$ : $$A \textbf{v}_{1} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 / \sqrt{2} \\ - 4 / \sqrt{2} \\ 4 / \sqrt{2} \end{bmatrix} , A \textbf{v}_{2} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}$$ As a check on the calculations, verify that $$\text{∥} A\textbf{v}_{1} \text{∥} = \sigma_{1} = 3\sqrt{2}$$ . Of course, $$A\textbf{v}_{2} = \textbf{0}$$ because $$\text{∥} \textit{A}\textbf{v}_{2} \text{∥} = \sigma_{2} = 0$$ . The only column found for $$U$$ so far is $$\textbf{u}_{1} = \frac{1}{3 \sqrt{2}} A \textbf{v}_{1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 / 3 \\ - 2 / 3 \\ 2 / 3 \end{bmatrix}$$ The other columns of $$U$$ are found by extending the set $$\left\{ \textbf{u}_{1} \text{\}} \right.$$ to an orthonormal basis for $${\mathbb{R}}^{3}$$ . In this case, we need two orthogonal unit vectors $$\textbf{u}_{2}$$ and $$\textbf{u}_{3}$$ that are orthogonal to $$\textbf{u}_{1}$$ . (See Figure 3.) Each vector must satisfy $$\textbf{u}_{1}^{T}\textbf{x} = 0$$ , which is equivalent to the equation $$x_{1} - 2x_{2} + 2x_{3} = 0$$ . A basis for the solution set of this equation is $$\textbf{w}_{1} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} , \textbf{w}_{2} = \begin{bmatrix} - 2 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$$ (Check that $$\textbf{w}_{1}$$ and $$\textbf{w}_{2}$$ are each orthogonal to $$\textbf{u}_{1}$$ .) Apply the Gram–Schmidt process (with normalizations) to $$\{\textbf{w}_{1},\textbf{w}_{2}\}$$ , and obtain $$\textbf{u}_{2} = \left[\right. 2 / \sqrt{5} 1 / \sqrt{5} 0 \left]\right. , \textbf{u}_{3} = \left[\right. - 2 / \sqrt{45} 4 / \sqrt{45} 5 / \sqrt{45} \left]\right.$$ Finally, set $$U = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{rrr} \textbf{u}_{1} & \textbf{u}_{2} & \textbf{u}_{3} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , take $$\text{Σ}$$ and $$V^{T}$$ from above, and write $$A = \left[\right. 1 & - 1 - 2 & 2 2 & - 2 \left]\right. = \left[\right. 1 / 3 & 2 / \sqrt{5} & - 2 / \sqrt{45} - 2 / 3 & 1 / \sqrt{5} & 4 / \sqrt{45} 2 / 3 & 0 & 5 / \sqrt{45} \left]\right. \left[\right. 3 \sqrt{2} & 0 0 & 0 0 & 0 \left]\right. \left[\right. 1 / \sqrt{2} & - 1 / \sqrt{2} 1 / \sqrt{2} & 1 / \sqrt{2} \left]\right.$$

title: (The Condition Number)
snippet: (The Condition Number): Example 5 (The Condition Number) Most numerical calculations involving an equation A\textbf{x} = \textbf{b} are as reliable as possible when the SVD of A is used. The two orthogonal matrices U and V do not affect...
body_xml:
<example number="5" title="(The Condition Number)">
    <heading level="2">Example 5 (The Condition Number)</heading>
    <paragraph>Most numerical calculations involving an equation $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{b}$$ are as reliable as possible when the SVD of $$A$$ is used. The two orthogonal matrices $$U$$ and $$V$$ do not affect lengths of vectors or angles between vectors (Theorem 7 in Section 6.2). Any possible instabilities in numerical calculations are identified in $$\text{Σ}$$ . If the singular values of $$A$$ are extremely large or small, roundoff errors are almost inevitable, but an error analysis is aided by knowing the entries in $$\text{Σ}$$ and $$V$$ .</paragraph>
    <paragraph>If $$A$$ is an invertible $$n \times n$$ matrix, then the ratio $$\sigma_{1}/\sigma_{n}$$ of the largest and smallest singular values gives the condition number of $$A$$ . Exercises 50–52 in Section 2.3 showed how the condition number affects the sensitivity of a solution of $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{b}$$ to changes (or errors) in the entries of $$A$$ . (Actually, a “condition number” of $$A$$ can be computed in several ways, but the definition given here is widely used for studying $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{b}$$ .)</paragraph>
  </example>

title: (Bases for Fundamental Subspaces)
snippet: (Bases for Fundamental Subspaces): Example 6 (Bases for Fundamental Subspaces) Given an SVD for an m \times n matrix A , let \textbf{u}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{u}_{m} be the left singular vectors, \textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{n} the right...
body_xml: Example 6 (Bases for Fundamental Subspaces) Given an SVD for an $$m \times n$$ matrix $$A$$ , let $$\textbf{u}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{u}_{m}$$ be the left singular vectors, $$\textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{n}$$ the right singular vectors, and $$\sigma_{1},\ldots,\sigma_{n}$$ the singular values, and let $$r$$ be the rank of $$A$$ . By Theorem 9, (5) $$\left{\right. \textbf{u}_{1} , \ldots , \textbf{u}_{r} \left.\right}$$ is an orthonormal basis for $$\text{Col} A$$ . Recall from Theorem 3 in Section 6.1 that $$\text{(Col} A)^{\bot} = \text{Nul} A^{T}$$ . Hence (6) $$\left{\right. \textbf{u}_{r + 1} , \ldots , \textbf{u}_{m} \left.\right}$$ is an orthonormal basis for $$\text{Nul} A^{T}$$ . Since $$\text{∥} \textit{A}\textbf{v}_{i} \text{∥} = \sigma_{i}$$ for $$1 \leq i \leq n$$ , and $$\sigma_{i}$$ is $$0$$ if and only if $$i > r$$ , the vectors $$\textbf{v}_{r + 1},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{n}$$ span a subspace of $$\text{Nul} A$$ of dimension $$n - r$$ . By the Rank Theorem, $$\dim \text{Nul} A = n - \text{rank} A$$ . It follows that (7) $$\left{\right. \textbf{v}_{r + 1} , \ldots , \textbf{v}_{n} \left.\right}$$ is an orthonormal basis for $$\text{Nul} A$$ , by the Basis Theorem (in Section 4.5). From (5) and (6), the orthogonal complement of $$\text{Nul} A^{T}$$ is $$\text{Col} A$$ . Interchanging $$A$$ and $$A^{T}$$ , note that $$\text{(Nul} A)^{\bot} = \text{Col} A^{T} = \text{Row} A$$ . Hence, from (7), (8) $$\left{\right. \textbf{v}_{1} , \ldots , \textbf{v}_{r} \left.\right}$$ is an orthonormal basis for $$\text{Row} A$$ . Figure 4 summarizes (5)–(8), but shows the orthogonal basis $$\{\sigma_{1}\textbf{u}_{1},\ldots,\sigma_{r}\textbf{u}_{r}\}$$ for $$\text{Col} A$$ instead of the normalized basis, to remind you that $$A\textbf{v}_{i} = \sigma_{i}\textbf{u}_{i}$$ for $$1 \leq i \leq r$$ . Explicit orthonormal bases for the four fundamental subspaces determined by $$A$$ are useful in some calculations, particularly in constrained optimization problems.

title: Theorem
snippet: Theorem: Theorem The Invertible Matrix Theorem (concluded) Let A be an n \times n matrix. Then the following statements are each equivalent to the statement that A is an invertible matrix: \text{(Col} A)^{\bot} = \text{\{} \textbf{0}...
body_xml:
<note type="procedure" source_type="procedure" title="Theorem">
    <heading level="2">Theorem</heading>
    <heading level="3">The Invertible Matrix Theorem (concluded)</heading>
    <paragraph>Let $$A$$ be an $$n \times n$$ matrix. Then the following statements are each equivalent to the statement that $$A$$ is an invertible matrix:</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>$$\text{(Col} A)^{\bot} = \text{\{} \textbf{0} \text{\}}$$ .</item>
      <item>$$\text{(Nul} A)^{\bot} = \mathbb{R}^{n}$$ .</item>
      <item>$$\text{Row} A = \mathbb{R}^{n}$$ .</item>
      <item>$$A$$ has $$n$$ nonzero singular values.</item>
    </list>
  </note>

title: (Reduced SVD and the Pseudoinverse of A)
snippet: (Reduced SVD and the Pseudoinverse of A): Example 7 (Reduced SVD and the Pseudoinverse of A) When \text{Σ} contains rows or columns of zeros, a more compact decomposition of A is possible. Using the notation established above, let r =...
body_xml:
<example number="7" title="(Reduced SVD and the Pseudoinverse of A)">
    <heading level="2">Example 7 (Reduced SVD and the Pseudoinverse of A)</heading>
    <paragraph>When $$\text{Σ}$$ contains rows or columns of zeros, a more compact decomposition of $$A$$ is possible. Using the notation established above, let $$r = \text{rank} A$$ , and partition $$U$$ and $$V$$ into submatrices whose first blocks contain $$r$$ columns:</paragraph>
    <paragraph>$$U = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}U_{r} & U_{m - r}\end{matrix} \left]\right. , & \text{where} U_{r} = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}\textbf{u}_{1} & \hdots & \textbf{u}_{r}\end{matrix} \left]\right. V = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}V_{r} & V_{n - r}\end{matrix} \left]\right. , & \text{where} V_{r} = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}\textbf{v}_{1} & \hdots & \textbf{v}_{r}\end{matrix} \left]\right.$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Then $$U_{r}$$ is $$m \times r$$ and $$V_{r}$$ is $$n \times r$$ . (To simplify notation, we consider $$U_{m - r}$$ or $$V_{n - r}$$ even though one of them may have no columns.) Then partitioned matrix multiplication shows that</paragraph>
    <paragraph>(9)</paragraph>
    <paragraph>$$A = \left[\right. U_{r} & U_{m - r} \left]\right. \left[\right. D & 0 0 & 0 \left]\right. \left[\right. V_{r}^{T} V_{n - r}^{T} \left]\right. = U_{r} D V_{r}^{T}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>This factorization of $$A$$ is called a reduced singular value decomposition of $$A$$ . Since the diagonal entries in $$D$$ are nonzero, $$D$$ is invertible. The following matrix is called the pseudoinverse (also, the Moore–Penrose inverse) of $$A$$ :</paragraph>
    <paragraph>(10)</paragraph>
    <paragraph>$$A^{+} = V_{r} D^{- 1} U_{r}^{T}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Supplementary Exercises 28–30 at the end of the chapter explore some of the properties of the reduced singular value decomposition and the pseudoinverse.</paragraph>
  </example>

title: (Least-Squares Solution)
snippet: (Least-Squares Solution): Example 8 (Least-Squares Solution) Given the equation A\textbf{x} = \textbf{b} , use the pseudoinverse of A in (10) to define \hat{\textbf{x}} = A^{+} \textbf{b} = V_{r} D^{- 1} U_{r}^{T} \textbf{b} Then, from the...
body_xml:
<example number="8" title="(Least-Squares Solution)">
    <heading level="2">Example 8 (Least-Squares Solution)</heading>
    <paragraph>Given the equation $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{b}$$ , use the pseudoinverse of $$A$$ in (10) to define</paragraph>
    <paragraph>$$\hat{\textbf{x}} = A^{+} \textbf{b} = V_{r} D^{- 1} U_{r}^{T} \textbf{b}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Then, from the SVD in (9),</paragraph>
    <paragraph>$$A \hat{\textbf{x}} & = \left(\right. U_{r} D V_{r}^{T} \left.\right) \left(\right. V_{r} D^{- 1} U_{r}^{T} \textbf{b} \left.\right) & = U_{r} \left(D D\right)^{- 1} U_{r}^{T} \textbf{b} \text{Because} V_{r}^{T} V_{r} = I_{r} & = U_{r} U_{r}^{T} \textbf{b}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>It follows from (5) that $$U_{r}U_{r}^{T}\textbf{b}$$ is the orthogonal projection $$\widehat{\textbf{b}}$$ of $$\textbf{b}$$ onto $$\text{Col} A$$ . (See Theorem 10 in Section 6.3.) Thus $$\widehat{\textbf{x}}$$ is a least-squares solution of $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{b}$$ . In fact, this $$\widehat{\textbf{x}}$$ has the smallest length among all least-squares solutions of $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{b}$$ . See Supplementary Exercise 30.</paragraph>
  </example>

body_xml: Example 1 An example of two-dimensional data is given by a set of weights and heights of $$N$$ college students. Let $$\textbf{X}_{j}$$ denote the observation vector in $$\mathbb{R}^{2}$$ that lists the weight and height of the $$j \text{th}$$ student. If $$w$$ denotes weight and $$h$$ height, then the matrix of observations has the form $$\left[\right. \begin{matrix}w_{1} & w_{2} & \hdots & w_{N} \\ h_{1} & h_{2} & \hdots & h_{N}\end{matrix} \left]\right. \uparrow \uparrow \uparrow \textbf{X}_{1} \textbf{X}_{2} \textbf{X}_{N}$$ The set of observation vectors can be visualized as a two-dimensional scatter plot. See Figure 1.

title: Example 2
snippet: Example 2: Example 2 The first three photographs of Railroad Valley, Nevada, shown in the chapter introduction can be viewed as one image of the region, with three spectral components, because simultaneous measurements of the region were...
body_xml: Example 2 The first three photographs of Railroad Valley, Nevada, shown in the chapter introduction can be viewed as one image of the region, with three spectral components, because simultaneous measurements of the region were made at three separate wavelengths. Each photograph gives different information about the same physical region. For instance, the first pixel in the upper-left corner of each photograph corresponds to the same place on the ground (about $$30$$ meters by $$30$$ meters). To each pixel there corresponds an observation vector in $$\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ that lists the signal intensities for that pixel in the three spectral bands. Typically, the image is $$2000 \times 2000$$ pixels, so there are $$4$$ million pixels in the image. The data for the image form a matrix with $$3$$ rows and $$4$$ million columns (with columns arranged in any convenient order). In this case, the “multidimensional” character of the data refers to the three spectral dimensions rather than the two spatial dimensions that naturally belong to any photograph. The data can be visualized as a cluster of $$4$$ million points in $$\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ , perhaps as in Figure 2. Figure 2 A scatter plot of spectral data for a satellite image

title: Example 3
snippet: Example 3: Example 3 Three measurements are made on each of four individuals in a random sample from a population. The observation vectors are \textbf{X}_{1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} , \textbf{X}_{2} = \begin{bmatrix} 4...
body_xml:
<example number="3">
    <heading level="2">Example 3</heading>
    <paragraph>Three measurements are made on each of four individuals in a random sample from a population. The observation vectors are</paragraph>
    <paragraph>$$\textbf{X}_{1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} , \textbf{X}_{2} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ 2 \\ 13 \end{bmatrix} , \textbf{X}_{3} = \begin{bmatrix} 7 \\ 8 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} , \textbf{X}_{4} = \begin{bmatrix} 8 \\ 4 \\ 5 \end{bmatrix}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Compute the sample mean and the covariance matrix.</paragraph>
    <heading level="3">Solution</heading>
    <paragraph>The sample mean is</paragraph>
    <paragraph>$$\textbf{M} = \frac{1}{4} \begin{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ 2 \\ 13 \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} 7 \\ 8 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} 8 \\ 4 \\ 5 \end{bmatrix} \end{bmatrix} = \frac{1}{4} \begin{bmatrix} 20 \\ 16 \\ 20 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ 4 \\ 5 \end{bmatrix}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Subtract the sample mean from $$\textbf{X}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{X}_{4}$$ to obtain</paragraph>
    <paragraph>$$\left(\hat{\textbf{X}}\right)_{1} = \begin{bmatrix} - 4 \\ - 2 \\ - 4 \end{bmatrix} , \left(\hat{\textbf{X}}\right)_{2} = \begin{bmatrix} - 1 \\ - 2 \\ 8 \end{bmatrix} , \left(\hat{\textbf{X}}\right)_{3} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 4 \\ - 4 \end{bmatrix} , \left(\hat{\textbf{X}}\right)_{4} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>and</paragraph>
    <paragraph>$$B = \begin{bmatrix} - 4 & - 1 & 2 & 3 \\ - 2 & - 2 & 4 & 0 \\ - 4 & 8 & - 4 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>The sample covariance matrix is</paragraph>
    <paragraph>$$S & = \frac{1}{3} \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}- 4 & - 1 & 2 & 3 \\ - 2 & - 2 & 4 & 0 \\ - 4 & 8 & - 4 & 0\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}- 4 & - 2 & - 4 \\ - 1 & - 2 & 8 \\ 2 & 4 & - 4 \\ 3 & 0 & 0\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} & = \frac{1}{3} \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}30 & 18 & 0 \\ 18 & 24 & - 24 \\ 0 & - 24 & 96\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}10 & 6 & 0 \\ 6 & 8 & - 8 \\ 0 & - 8 & 32\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix}$$</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Example 4
snippet: Example 4: Example 4 The initial data for the multispectral image of Railroad Valley (Example 2) consisted of 4 million vectors in \mathbb{R}^{3} . The associated covariance matrix is1 S = \begin{bmatrix} 2382.78 & 2611.84 & 2136.20 \\...
body_xml:
<example number="4">
    <heading level="2">Example 4</heading>
    <paragraph>The initial data for the multispectral image of Railroad Valley (Example 2) consisted of $$4$$ million vectors in $$\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ . The associated covariance matrix is1</paragraph>
    <paragraph>$$S = \begin{bmatrix} 2382.78 & 2611.84 & 2136.20 \\ 2611.84 & 3106.47 & 2553.90 \\ 2136.20 & 2553.90 & 2650.71 \end{bmatrix}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Find the principal components of the data, and list the new variable determined by the first principal component.</paragraph>
    <heading level="3">Solution</heading>
    <paragraph>The eigenvalues of $$S$$ and the associated principal components (the unit eigenvectors) are</paragraph>
    <paragraph>$$\lambda_{1} & = 7614.23 & \lambda_{2} & = 427.63 & \lambda_{3} & = 98.10 \textbf{u}_{1} & = \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}.5417 \\ .6295 \\ .5570\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} & \textbf{u}_{2} & = \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}- .4894 \\ - .3026 \\ .8179\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} & \textbf{u}_{3} & = \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}.6834 \\ - .7157 \\ .1441\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Using two decimal places for simplicity, the variable for the first principal component is</paragraph>
    <paragraph>$$y_{1} = .54 x_{1} + .63 x_{2} + .56 x_{3}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>This equation was used to create photograph (d) in the chapter introduction. The variables $$x_{1}$$ , $$x_{2}$$ , and $$x_{3}$$ are the signal intensities in the three spectral bands. The values of $$x_{1}$$ , converted to a gray scale between black and white, produced photograph (a). Similarly, the values of $$x_{2}$$ and $$x_{3}$$ produced photographs (b) and (c), respectively. At each pixel in photograph (d), the gray scale value is computed from $$y_{1}$$ , a weighted linear combination of $$x_{1},x_{2},$$ and $$x_{3}$$ . In this sense, photograph (d) “displays” the first principal component of the data.</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Example 5
snippet: Example 5: Example 5 Compute the various percentages of variance of the Railroad Valley multispectral data that are displayed in the principal component photographs, (d)–(f), shown in the chapter introduction. Solution The total variance...
body_xml:
<example number="5">
    <heading level="2">Example 5</heading>
    <paragraph>Compute the various percentages of variance of the Railroad Valley multispectral data that are displayed in the principal component photographs, (d)–(f), shown in the chapter introduction.</paragraph>
    <heading level="3">Solution</heading>
    <paragraph>The total variance of the data is</paragraph>
    <paragraph>$$\text{tr} \left(\right. D \left.\right) = 7614.23 + 427.63 + 98.10 = 8139.96$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>[Verify that this number also equals $$\text{tr} (S)$$ .] The percentages of the total variance explained by the principal components are</paragraph>
    <paragraph>$$\text{First} \text{component} & \text{Second} \text{component} & \text{Third} \text{component} \frac{7614.23}{8139.96} = 93.5 \% & \frac{427.63}{8139.96} = 5.3 \% & \frac{98.10}{8139.96} = 1.2 \%$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>In a sense, $$93.5\%$$ of the information collected by Landsat for the Railroad Valley region is displayed in photograph (d), with $$5.3\%$$ in (e) and only $$1.2\%$$ remaining for (f).</paragraph>
  </example>

<note type="definition" source_type="definition" title="﻿Definition">
    <heading level="2">﻿Definition</heading>
    <paragraph>The set of all affine combinations of points in a set $$S$$ is called the affine hull (or affine span) of $$S,$$ denoted by $$\text{aff} S$$ .﻿</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Theorem 1
snippet: Theorem 1: Theorem 1 A point \textbf{y} in \mathbb{R}^{n} is an affine combination of \textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{p} in \mathbb{R}^{n} if and only if \textbf{y} - \textbf{v}_{1} is a linear combination of the translated points...
body_xml:
<note type="procedure" source_type="procedure" title="Theorem 1">
    <heading level="2">Theorem 1</heading>
    <paragraph>A point $$\textbf{y}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ is an affine combination of $$\textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{p}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ if and only if $$\textbf{y} - \textbf{v}_{1}$$ is a linear combination of the translated points $$\textbf{v}_{2} - \textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{p} - \textbf{v}_{1}$$ .﻿</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Example 1
snippet: Example 1: Example 1 Let \mathbf{v}_{1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} , \mathbf{v}_{2} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 5 \end{bmatrix} , \mathbf{v}_{3} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix} , \mathbf{v}_{4} = \begin{bmatrix} {- 2} \\ 2...
body_xml:
<example number="1">
    <heading level="2">Example 1</heading>
    <paragraph>Let $$\mathbf{v}_{1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}$$ , $$\mathbf{v}_{2} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 5 \end{bmatrix}$$ , $$\mathbf{v}_{3} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}$$ , $$\mathbf{v}_{4} = \begin{bmatrix} {- 2} \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}$$ , and $$\text{y} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$$ . If possible, write $$\textbf{y}$$ as an affine combination of $$\textbf{v}_{1}$$ , $$\textbf{v}_{2}$$ , $$\textbf{v}_{3}$$ and $$\textbf{v}_{4}$$ .﻿</paragraph>
    <heading level="3">Solution</heading>
    <paragraph>Compute the translated points</paragraph>
    <paragraph>$$\mathbf{v}_{2} - \mathbf{v}_{1} = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}1 \\ 3\end{matrix} \left]\right. , & \mathbf{v}_{3} - \mathbf{v}_{1} = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}0 \\ 1\end{matrix} \left]\right. , & \mathbf{v}_{4} - \mathbf{v}_{1} = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}- 3 \\ 0\end{matrix} \left]\right. , & \mathbf{y} - \mathbf{v}_{1} = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}3 \\ - 1\end{matrix} \left]\right.$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>To find scalars $$c_{2}$$ , $$c_{3}$$ , and $$c_{4}$$ such that</paragraph>
    <paragraph>(5)</paragraph>
    <paragraph>$$c_{2} \left(\right. \textbf{v}_{2} - \textbf{v}_{1} \left.\right) + c_{3} \left(\right. \textbf{v}_{3} - \textbf{v}_{1} \left.\right) + c_{4} \left(\right. \textbf{v}_{4} - \textbf{v}_{1} \left.\right) = \textbf{y} - \textbf{v}_{1}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>row reduce the augmented matrix having these points as columns:</paragraph>
    <paragraph>$$\left[\right. 1 & 0 & - 3 & 3 3 & 1 & 0 & - 1 \left]\right. sim \left[\right. 1 & 0 & - 3 & 3 0 & 1 & 9 & - 10 \left]\right.$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>This shows that equation (5) is consistent, and the general solution is $$c_{2} = 3c_{4} + 3$$ , $$c_{3} = - 9c_{4} - 10$$ , with $$c_{4}$$ free. When $$c_{4} = 0$$ .﻿</paragraph>
    <paragraph>$$y - v_{1} = 3 \left(\right. v_{2} - v_{1} \left.\right) - 10 \left(\right. v_{3} - v_{1} \left.\right) + 0 \left(\right. v_{4} - v_{1} \left.\right)$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>and</paragraph>
    <paragraph>$$y = 8 v_{1} + 3 v_{2} - 10 v_{3}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>As another example, take $$c_{4} = 1$$ . Then $$c_{2} = 6$$ and $$c_{3} = - 19$$ , so</paragraph>
    <paragraph>$$\textbf{y} - \textbf{v}_{1} = 6 \left(\right. \textbf{v}_{2} - \textbf{v}_{1} \left.\right) - 19 \left(\right. \textbf{v}_{3} - \textbf{v}_{1} \left.\right) + 1 \left(\right. \textbf{v}_{4} - \textbf{v}_{1} \left.\right)$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>and</paragraph>
    <paragraph>$$y = 13 v_{1} + 6 v_{2} - 19 v_{3} + v_{4}$$</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Example 2
snippet: Example 2: Example 2 Let b_{1} = \left[\right. 4 0 3 \left]\right. , b_{2} = \left[\right. 0 4 2 \left]\right. , b_{3} = \left[\right. 5 2 4 \left]\right. , {\mathbf{p}_{1} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}}, and \mathbf{p}_{2} =...
body_xml:
<example number="2">
    <heading level="2">Example 2</heading>
    <paragraph>Let $$b_{1} = \left[\right. 4 0 3 \left]\right. ,$$ $$b_{2} = \left[\right. 0 4 2 \left]\right. ,$$ $$b_{3} = \left[\right. 5 2 4 \left]\right. ,$$ $${\mathbf{p}_{1} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}},$$ and $$\mathbf{p}_{2} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}$$ . The set $$B = \{\textbf{b}_{1},\textbf{b}_{2},\textbf{b}_{3}\}$$ is a basis for $$\mathbb{R}^{3}.$$ Determine whether the points $$\textbf{p}_{1}$$ and $$\textbf{p}_{2}$$ are affine combinations of the points in $$B$$ .﻿</paragraph>
    <heading level="3">Solution</heading>
    <paragraph>Find the $$B \text{-coordinates}$$ of $$\textbf{p}_{1}$$ and $$\textbf{p}_{2}$$ . These two calculations can be combined by row reducing the matrix $$\left\lbrack \begin{array}{lllll} \mathbf{b}_{1} & \mathbf{b}_{2} & \mathbf{b}_{3} & \mathbf{p}_{1} & \mathbf{p}_{2} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , with two augmented columns:</paragraph>
    <paragraph>$$\left[\right. 4 & 0 & 5 & 2 & 1 0 & 4 & 2 & 0 & 2 3 & 2 & 4 & 0 & 2 \left]\right. ∼ \left[\right. 1 & 0 & 0 & - 2 & \frac{2}{3} 0 & 1 & 0 & - 1 & \frac{2}{3} 0 & 0 & 1 & 2 & - \frac{1}{3} \left]\right.$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Read column $$4$$ to build $$\textbf{p}_{1}$$ , and read column $$5$$ to build $$\textbf{p}_{2}$$ :</paragraph>
    <paragraph>$$\mathbf{p}_{1} = - 2 \mathbf{b}_{1} - \mathbf{b}_{2} + 2 \mathbf{b}_{3} & \text{and} & \mathbf{p}_{2} = \frac{2}{3} \mathbf{b}_{1} + \frac{2}{3} \mathbf{b}_{2} - \frac{1}{3} \mathbf{b}_{3}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>The sum of the weights in the linear combination for $$\textbf{p}_{1}$$ is $$- 1$$ , not $$1$$ , so $$\textbf{p}_{1}$$ is not an affine combination of the $$\textbf{b}$$ ’s. However, $$\textbf{p}_{2}$$ is an affine combination of the $$\textbf{b}$$ ’s, because the sum of the weights for $$\textbf{p}_{2}$$ is $$1$$ .﻿</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Definition
snippet: Definition: Definition A set S is affine if \textbf{p} , \textbf{q} \in S implies that (1 - t)\textbf{p} + t\textbf{q} \in S for each real number t .﻿
body_xml:
<note type="definition" source_type="definition" title="Definition">
    <heading level="2">Definition</heading>
    <paragraph>A set $$S$$ is affine if $$\textbf{p}$$ , $$\textbf{q} \in S$$ implies that $$(1 - t)\textbf{p} + t\textbf{q} \in S$$ for each real number $$t$$ .﻿</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Theorem 2
snippet: Theorem 2: Theorem 2 A set S is affine if and only if every affine combination of points of S lies in S . That is, S is affine if and only if S = \text{aff} S .﻿
body_xml:
<note type="procedure" source_type="procedure" title="Theorem 2">
    <heading level="2">Theorem 2</heading>
    <paragraph>A set $$S$$ is affine if and only if every affine combination of points of $$S$$ lies in $$S$$ . That is, $$S$$ is affine if and only if $$S = \text{aff} S$$ .﻿</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Definition
snippet: Definition: Definition A translate of a set S in \mathbb{R}^{n} by a vector \textbf{p} is the set S + \textbf{p} = \left{\right. \textbf{s} + \textbf{p} : \textbf{s} \in S \left.\right} .﻿2 A flat in \mathbb{R}^{n} is a translate of a...
body_xml:
<note type="definition" source_type="definition" title="Definition">
    <heading level="2">Definition</heading>
    <paragraph>A translate of a set $$S$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ by a vector $$\textbf{p}$$ is the set $$S + \textbf{p} = \left{\right. \textbf{s} + \textbf{p} : \textbf{s} \in S \left.\right}$$ .﻿2 A flat in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ is a translate of a subspace of $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ . Two flats are parallel if one is a translate of the other. The dimension of a flat is the dimension of the corresponding parallel subspace. The dimension of a set $$S$$ , written as dim $$S$$ , is the dimension of the smallest flat containing $$S$$ . A line in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ is a flat of dimension $$1$$ . A hyperplane in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ is a flat of dimension $$n - 1$$ .﻿</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Theorem 3
snippet: Theorem 3: Theorem 3 A nonempty set S is affine if and only if it is a flat.
body_xml:
<note type="procedure" source_type="procedure" title="Theorem 3">
    <heading level="2">Theorem 3</heading>
    <paragraph>A nonempty set $$S$$ is affine if and only if it is a flat.</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Example 3
snippet: Example 3: Example 3 Suppose that the solutions of an equation A\textbf{x} = \textbf{b} are all of the form \textbf{x} = x_{3}\textbf{u} + \textbf{p} , where \mathbf{u} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 2 \\ {- 3} \\ 1 \end{array}...
body_xml:
<example number="3">
    <heading level="2">Example 3</heading>
    <paragraph>Suppose that the solutions of an equation $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{b}$$ are all of the form $$\textbf{x} = x_{3}\textbf{u} + \textbf{p}$$ , where $$\mathbf{u} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 2 \\ {- 3} \\ 1 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ and $$\mathbf{p} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ 0 \\ {- 3} \end{bmatrix}$$ , Recall from Section 1.5 that this set is parallel to the solution set of $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{0}$$ , which consists of all points of the form $$x_{3}\textbf{u}$$ . Find points $$\textbf{v}_{1}$$ and $$\textbf{v}_{2}$$ such that the solution set of $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{b}$$ is $$\text{aff} \left\{ \textbf{v}_{1},\textbf{v}_{2} \right\}$$ .﻿</paragraph>
    <heading level="3">Solution</heading>
    <paragraph>The solution set is a line through $$\textbf{p}$$ in the direction of $$\textbf{u}$$ , as in Figure 1. Since $$\text{aff} \{\textbf{v}_{1},\textbf{v}_{2}\}$$ is a line through $$\textbf{v}_{1}$$ and $$\textbf{v}_{2}$$ , identify two points on the line $$\textbf{x} = x_{3}\textbf{u} + \textbf{p}$$ . Two simple choices appear when $$x_{3} = 0$$ and $$x_{3} = 1$$ . That is, take $$\textbf{v}_{1} = \textbf{p}$$ and $$\textbf{v}_{2} = \textbf{u} + \textbf{p}$$ , so that</paragraph>
    <paragraph>$$v_{2} = u + p = \left[\right. 2 - 3 1 \left]\right. + \left[\right. 4 0 - 3 \left]\right. = \left[\right. 6 - 3 - 2 \left]\right.$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>In this case, the solution set is described as the set of all affine combinations of the form</paragraph>
    <paragraph>$$x = \left(\right. 1 - x_{3} \left.\right) \left[\right. 4 0 - 3 \left]\right. + x_{3} \left[\right. 6 - 3 - 2 \left]\right.$$</paragraph>
  </example>

  </note>

title: Theorem 4
snippet: Theorem 4: Theorem 4 A point \textbf{y} in \mathbb{R}^{n} is an affine combination of \textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{p} in \mathbb{R}^{n} if and only if the homogeneous form of \textbf{y} is in \text{Span\{}...
body_xml:
<note type="procedure" source_type="procedure" title="Theorem 4">
    <heading level="2">Theorem 4</heading>
    <paragraph>A point $$\textbf{y}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ is an affine combination of $$\textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{p}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ if and only if the homogeneous form of $$\textbf{y}$$ is in $$\text{Span\{} {\overset{\sim}{\textbf{v}}}_{1},\ldots,{\overset{\sim}{\textbf{v}}}_{p} \text{\}}$$ . In fact, $$\textbf{y} = c_{1}\textbf{v}_{1} + \cdots + c_{p}\textbf{v}_{p}$$ , with $$c_{1} + \cdots + c_{p} = 1$$ , if and only if $$\overset{\sim}{\textbf{y}} = c_{1}{\overset{\sim}{\textbf{v}}}_{1} + \cdots + c_{p}{\overset{\sim}{\textbf{v}}}_{p}$$ .﻿</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Example 4
snippet: Example 4: Example 4 Let \mathbf{v}_{1} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} , \mathbf{v}_{2} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} , \mathbf{v}_{3} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 7 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} , and \mathbf{p} =...
body_xml: Example 4 Let $$\mathbf{v}_{1} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$$ , $$\mathbf{v}_{2} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}$$ , $$\mathbf{v}_{3} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 7 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$$ , and $$\mathbf{p} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ 3 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}$$ . Use Theorem 4 to write $$\textbf{p}$$ as an affine combination of $$\textbf{v}_{1}$$ , $$\textbf{v}_{2}$$ , and $$\textbf{v}_{3}$$ , if possible. Solution Row reduce the augmented matrix for the equation $$x_{1} \left(\overset{\sim}{\textbf{v}}\right)_{1} + x_{2} \left(\overset{\sim}{\textbf{v}}\right)_{2} + x_{3} \left(\overset{\sim}{\textbf{v}}\right)_{3} = \overset{\sim}{\textbf{p}}$$ To simplify the arithmetic, move the fourth row of 1’s to the top (equivalent to three row interchanges). After this, the number of arithmetic operations here is basically the same as the number needed for the method using Theorem 1. $$\begin{matrix}\left[\right. \begin{matrix}\left(\overset{\sim}{\textbf{v}}\right)_{1} & \left(\overset{\sim}{\textbf{v}}\right)_{2} & \left(\overset{\sim}{\textbf{v}}\right)_{3} & \overset{\sim}{p}\end{matrix} \left]\right. ∼ & \left[\right. \begin{matrix}1 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 3 & 1 & 1 & 4 \\ 1 & 2 & 7 & 3 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 & 0\end{matrix} \left]\right. ∼ & \left[\right. \begin{matrix}1 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & - 2 & - 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 6 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & - 1\end{matrix} \left]\right.\end{matrix} ∼ \hdots ∼ \left[\right. \begin{matrix}1 & 0 & 0 & 1.5 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & - 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & .5 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{matrix} \left]\right.$$ By Theorem 4, $$1.5\textbf{v}_{1} - \textbf{v}_{2} + .5\textbf{v}_{3} = \textbf{p}$$ . See Figure 4, which shows the plane that contains $$\textbf{v}_{1}$$ , $$\textbf{v}_{2}$$ , $$\textbf{v}_{3}$$ , and $$\textbf{p}$$ (together with points on the coordinate axes).

title: Definition
snippet: Definition: Definition An indexed set of points \{\textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{p}\} in \mathbb{R}^{n} is affinely dependent if there exist real numbers c_{1},\ldots,c_{p} , not all zero, such that (1) c_{1} + \hdots + c_{p} = 0 and...
body_xml:
<note type="definition" source_type="definition" title="Definition">
    <heading level="2">Definition</heading>
    <paragraph>An indexed set of points $$\{\textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{p}\}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ is affinely dependent if there exist real numbers $$c_{1},\ldots,c_{p}$$ , not all zero, such that</paragraph>
    <paragraph>(1)</paragraph>
    <paragraph>$$c_{1} + \hdots + c_{p} = 0 and c_{1} \textbf{v}_{1} + \hdots + c_{p} \textbf{v}_{p} = \textbf{0}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Otherwise, the set is affinely independent.</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Theorem ﻿5﻿
snippet: Theorem ﻿5﻿: Theorem ﻿5﻿ Given an indexed set S = \{\textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{p}\} in \mathbb{R}^{n} , with p \geq 2 , the following statements are logically equivalent. That is, either they are all true statements or they are all...
body_xml:
<note type="procedure" source_type="procedure" title="Theorem ﻿5﻿">
    <heading level="2">Theorem ﻿5﻿</heading>
    <paragraph>Given an indexed set $$S = \{\textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{p}\}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ , with $$p \geq 2$$ , the following statements are logically equivalent. That is, either they are all true statements or they are all false.</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>$$S$$ is affinely dependent.</item>
      <item>One of the points in $$S$$ is an affine combination of the other points in $$S$$ .﻿</item>
      <item>The set $$\{\textbf{v}_{2} - \textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{p} - \textbf{v}_{1}\}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ is linearly dependent.</item>
      <item>The set $$\{{\widetilde{\textbf{v}}}_{1},\ldots,{\widetilde{\textbf{v}}}_{p}\}$$ of homogeneous forms in $$\mathbb{R}^{n + 1}$$ is linearly dependent.</item>
    </list>
  </note>

title: Example 1
snippet: Example 1: Example 1 The affine hull of two distinct points \textbf{p} and \textbf{q} is a line. If a third point \textbf{r} is on the line, then \{\textbf{p},\textbf{q},\textbf{r}\} is an affinely dependent set. If a point \textbf{s} is...
body_xml: Example 1 The affine hull of two distinct points $$\textbf{p}$$ and $$\textbf{q}$$ is a line. If a third point $$\textbf{r}$$ is on the line, then $$\{\textbf{p},\textbf{q},\textbf{r}\}$$ is an affinely dependent set. If a point $$\textbf{s}$$ is not on the line through $$\textbf{p}$$ and $$\textbf{q}$$ , then these three points are not collinear and $$\{\textbf{p},\textbf{q},\textbf{s}\}$$ is an affinely independent set. See Figure 1.

title: Example 2
snippet: Example 2: Example 2 Let \textbf{v}_{1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \\ 7 \end{bmatrix} , \mathbf{v}_{2} = \left[\right. 2 7 6.5 \left]\right. , \textbf{v}_{3} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 4 \\ 7 \end{bmatrix}, and S = \left\{...
body_xml: Example 2 Let $$\textbf{v}_{1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \\ 7 \end{bmatrix} ,$$ $$\mathbf{v}_{2} = \left[\right. 2 7 6.5 \left]\right. ,$$ $$\textbf{v}_{3} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 4 \\ 7 \end{bmatrix},$$ and $$S = \left\{ \textbf{v}_{1},\textbf{v}_{2},\textbf{v}_{3} \right\}$$ . Determine whether $$S$$ is affinely independent. Solution Compute $$\mathbf{v}_{2} - \mathbf{v}_{1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 4 \\ {- .5} \end{bmatrix}$$ and $$\textbf{v}_{3} - \textbf{v}_{1} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} {- 1} \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{array} \right\rbrack.$$ These two points are not multiples and hence form a linearly independent set, $$S\prime$$ . So all statements in Theorem 5 are false, and $$S$$ is affinely independent. Figure 2 shows $$S$$ and the translated set $$S\prime$$ . Notice that $$\text{Span} S\prime$$ is a plane through the origin and $$\text{aff} S$$ is a parallel plane through $$\textbf{v}_{1}$$ , $$\textbf{v}_{2}$$ , and $$\textbf{v}_{3}$$ . (Only a portion of each plane is shown here, of course.)

title: Example 3
snippet: Example 3: Example 3 Let \textbf{v}_{1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \\ 7 \end{bmatrix} , \mathbf{v}_{2} = \left[\right. 2 7 6.5 \left]\right. , \textbf{v}_{3} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 4 \\ 7 \end{bmatrix}, and \textbf{v}_{4} = \left\lbrack...
body_xml:
<example number="3">
    <heading level="2">Example 3</heading>
    <paragraph>Let $$\textbf{v}_{1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \\ 7 \end{bmatrix} ,$$ $$\mathbf{v}_{2} = \left[\right. 2 7 6.5 \left]\right. ,$$ $$\textbf{v}_{3} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 4 \\ 7 \end{bmatrix},$$ and $$\textbf{v}_{4} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 0 \\ 14 \\ 6 \end{array} \right\rbrack,$$ and let $$S = \left\{ \textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{4} \right\}$$ . Is $$S$$ affinely dependent?</paragraph>
    <heading level="3">Solution</heading>
    <paragraph>Compute $$\textbf{v}_{2} - \textbf{v}_{1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 4 \\ - .5 \end{bmatrix} ,$$ $$\textbf{v}_{3} - \textbf{v}_{1} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} {- 1} \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{array} \right\rbrack,$$ and $$\textbf{v}_{4} - \textbf{v}_{1} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} {- 1} \\ 11 \\ {- 1} \end{array} \right\rbrack,$$ and row reduce the matrix:</paragraph>
    <paragraph>$$\left[\right. 1 & - 1 & - 1 4 & 1 & 11 - .5 & 0 & - 1 \left]\right. sim \left[\right. 1 & - 1 & - 1 0 & 5 & 15 0 & - .5 & - 1.5 \left]\right. sim \left[\right. 1 & - 1 & - 1 0 & 5 & 15 0 & 0 & 0 \left]\right.$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Recall from Section 4.5 (or Section 2.8) that the columns are linearly dependent because not every column is a pivot column; so $$\textbf{v}_{2} - \textbf{v}_{1}$$ , $$\textbf{v}_{3} - \textbf{v}_{1}$$ , and $$\textbf{v}_{4} - \textbf{v}_{1}$$ are linearly dependent. By statement (c) in Theorem 5, $$\{\textbf{v}_{1},\textbf{v}_{2},\textbf{v}_{3},\textbf{v}_{4}\}$$ is affinely dependent. This dependence can also be established using (d) in Theorem 5 instead of (c).</paragraph>
  </example>

Then each $$\textbf{p}$$ in $$\text{aff} S$$ has a unique representation as an affine combination of $$\textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{k}$$ . That is, for each $$\textbf{p}$$ there exists a unique set of scalars $$c_{1},\ldots,c_{k}$$ such that</paragraph>
    <paragraph>(7)</paragraph>
    <paragraph>$$\textbf{p} = c_{1} \textbf{v}_{1} + \hdots + c_{k} \textbf{v}_{k} and c_{1} + \hdots + c_{k} = 1$$</paragraph>
  </note>

Then for each point $$\textbf{p}$$ in $$\text{aff} S$$ , the coefficients $$c_{1},\ldots,c_{k}$$ in the unique representation (7) of $$\textbf{p}$$ are called the barycentric coordinates (or, sometimes, affine) of $$\textbf{p}$$ .﻿</paragraph>

title: Example 4
snippet: Example 4: Example 4 Let \textbf{a} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 7 \end{bmatrix} , \textbf{b} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} , \textbf{c} = \begin{bmatrix} 9 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix} , and \textbf{p} = \begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix} ....
body_xml:
<example number="4">
    <heading level="2">Example 4</heading>
    <paragraph>Let $$\textbf{a} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 7 \end{bmatrix}$$ , $$\textbf{b} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}$$ , $$\textbf{c} = \begin{bmatrix} 9 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}$$ , and $$\textbf{p} = \begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}$$ . Find the barycentric coordinates of $$\textbf{p}$$ determined by the affinely independent set $$\left\{ \textbf{a},\textbf{b},\textbf{c} \right\}$$ .﻿</paragraph>
    <heading level="3">Solution</heading>
    <paragraph>Row reduce the augmented matrix of points in homogeneous form, moving the last row of ones to the top to simplify the arithmetic:</paragraph>
    <paragraph>$$\begin{matrix}\begin{matrix}\left[\right. \begin{matrix}\overset{\sim}{\mathbf{a}} & \overset{\sim}{\mathbf{b}} & \overset{\sim}{\mathbf{c}} & \overset{\sim}{p}\end{matrix} \left]\right. = & \left[\right. \begin{matrix}1 & 3 & 9 & 5 \\ 7 & 0 & 3 & 3 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 & 1\end{matrix} \left]\right. ∼ & \left[\right. \begin{matrix}1 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 & 9 & 5 \\ 7 & 0 & 3 & 3\end{matrix} \left]\right.\end{matrix} \\ ∼ \left[\right. \begin{matrix}1 & 0 & 0 & \frac{1}{4} \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & \frac{1}{3} \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & \frac{5}{12}\end{matrix} \left]\right.\end{matrix}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>The coordinates are $$\frac{1}{4}$$ , $$\frac{1}{3}$$ , and $$\frac{5}{12}$$ , so $$\textbf{p} = \frac{1}{4}\textbf{a} + \frac{1}{3}\textbf{b} + \frac{5}{12}\textbf{c}$$ .﻿</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Example 5
snippet: Example 5: Example 5 Let \textbf{v}_{1} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 1 \\ 5 \end{bmatrix} , \textbf{v}_{2} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ 3 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix} , \textbf{v}_{3} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 5 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}, and \textbf{p} = \begin{bmatrix}...
body_xml: Example 5 Let $$\textbf{v}_{1} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 1 \\ 5 \end{bmatrix} ,$$ $$\textbf{v}_{2} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ 3 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix} ,$$ $$\textbf{v}_{3} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 5 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix},$$ and $$\textbf{p} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 3 \\ 3.5 \end{bmatrix}.$$ The colors at the vertices $$\textbf{v}_{1}$$ , $$\textbf{v}_{2}$$ , and $$\textbf{v}_{3}$$ of a triangle are magenta $$(1,0,1)$$ , light magenta $$(1,.4,1)$$ , and purple $$(.6,0,1)$$ , respectively. Find the interpolated color at $$\textbf{p}$$ . See Figure 6. Solution First, find the barycentric coordinates of $$\textbf{p}$$ . Here is the calculation using homogeneous forms of the points, with the first step moving row $$4$$ to row $$1$$ : $$\left[\right. \begin{matrix}\overset{\sim}{v}_{1} & \overset{\sim}{v}_{2} & \overset{\sim}{v}_{3} & \overset{\sim}{p}\end{matrix} \left]\right. & sim & \left[\right. \begin{matrix}1 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 3 & 4 & 1 & 3 \\ 1 & 3 & 5 & 3 \\ 5 & 4 & 1 & 3.5\end{matrix} \left]\right. & sim & \left[\right. \begin{matrix}1 & 0 & 0 & .25 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & .50 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & .25 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{matrix} \left]\right.$$ So $$\textbf{p} = .25\textbf{v}_{1} + .5\textbf{v}_{2} + .25\textbf{v}_{3}$$ . Use the barycentric coordinates of $$\textbf{p}$$ to make a linear combination of the color data. The RGB values for $$\textbf{p}$$ are $$.25 \left[\right. 1 0 1 \left]\right. + .50 \left[\right. 1 .4 1 \left]\right. + .25 \left[\right. .6 0 1 \left]\right. = \left[\right. .9 .2 1 \left]\right. \text{red} \text{green} \text{blue}$$

title: Example 6
snippet: Example 6: Example 6 Let v_{1} = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}1 \\ 1 \\ - 6\end{matrix} \left]\right. , & & v_{2} = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}8 \\ 1 \\ - 4\end{matrix} \left]\right. , & & v_{3} = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}5 \\ 11 \\ -...
body_xml:
<example number="6">
    <heading level="2">Example 6</heading>
    <paragraph>Let</paragraph>
    <paragraph>$$v_{1} = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}1 \\ 1 \\ - 6\end{matrix} \left]\right. , & & v_{2} = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}8 \\ 1 \\ - 4\end{matrix} \left]\right. , & & v_{3} = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}5 \\ 11 \\ - 2\end{matrix} \left]\right. , & & a = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 10\end{matrix} \left]\right. , & & b = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}.7 \\ .4 \\ - 3\end{matrix} \left]\right. ,$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>and $$\textbf{x}(t) = \textbf{a} + t\textbf{b}$$ for $$t \geq 0$$ . Find the point where the ray $$\textbf{x}(t)$$ intersects the plane that contains the triangle with vertices $$\textbf{v}_{1}$$ , $$\textbf{v}_{2}$$ , and $$\textbf{v}_{3}$$ . Is this point inside the triangle?</paragraph>
    <heading level="3">Solution</heading>
    <paragraph>The plane is $$\text{aff} \left\{ \textbf{v}_{1},\textbf{v}_{2},\textbf{v}_{3} \right\}$$ . A typical point in this plane may be written as $$(1 - c_{2} - c_{3})\textbf{v}_{1} + c_{2}\textbf{v}_{2} + c_{3}\textbf{v}_{3}$$ for some $$c_{2}$$ and $$c_{3}$$ . (The weights in this combination sum to $$1$$ .) The ray $$\textbf{x}(t)$$ intersects the plane when $$c_{2}$$ , $$c_{3}$$ , and $$t$$ satisfy</paragraph>
    <paragraph>$$\left(\right. 1 - c_{2} - c_{3} \left.\right) \textbf{v}_{1} + c_{2} \textbf{v}_{2} + c_{3} \textbf{v}_{3} = \textbf{a} + t \textbf{b}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Rearrange this as $$c_{2}\left( \textbf{v}_{2} - \textbf{v}_{1} \right) + c_{3}\left( \textbf{v}_{3} - \textbf{v}_{1} \right) + t\left( - \textbf{b} \right) = \textbf{a} - \textbf{v}_{1}$$ . In matrix form,</paragraph>
    <paragraph>$$[ \begin{matrix}\mathbf{v}_{2} - \mathbf{v}_{1} & \mathbf{v}_{3} - \mathbf{v}_{1} & - \mathbf{b}\end{matrix} ] & \left[\right. \begin{matrix}c_{2} \\ c_{3} \\ t\end{matrix} \left]\right. & = & \mathbf{a} - \mathbf{v}_{1}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>For the specific points given here,</paragraph>
    <paragraph>$$v_{2} - v_{1} = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}7 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{matrix} \left]\right. , & v_{3} - v_{1} = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}4 \\ 10 \\ 4\end{matrix} \left]\right. , & a - v_{1} = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}- 1 \\ - 1 \\ 16\end{matrix} \left]\right.$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Row reduction of the augmented matrix above produces</paragraph>
    <paragraph>$$\left[\right. \begin{matrix}7 & 4 & - .7 & - 1 \\ 0 & 10 & - .4 & - 1 \\ 2 & 4 & 3 & 16\end{matrix} \left]\right. & \sim & \left[\right. \begin{matrix}1 & 0 & 0 & .3 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & .1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 5\end{matrix} \left]\right.$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Thus $$c_{2} = .3$$ , $$c_{3} = .1$$ , and $$t = 5$$ . Therefore, the intersection point is</paragraph>
    <paragraph>$$x \left(\right. 5 \left.\right) = a + 5 b = \left[\right. 0 0 10 \left]\right. + 5 \left[\right. .7 .4 - 3 \left]\right. = \left[\right. 3.5 2.0 - 5.0 \left]\right.$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Also,</paragraph>
    <paragraph>$$\mathbf{x} \left(\right. 5 \left.\right) & = & \left(\right. 1 - .3 - .1 \left.\right) \mathbf{v}_{1} + .3 \mathbf{v}_{2} + .1 \mathbf{v}_{3} & = & .6 \left[\right. \begin{matrix}1 \\ 1 \\ - 6\end{matrix} \left]\right. + .3 \left[\right. \begin{matrix}8 \\ 1 \\ - 4\end{matrix} \left]\right. + .1 \left[\right. \begin{matrix}5 \\ 11 \\ - 2\end{matrix} \left]\right. = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}3.5 \\ 2.0 \\ - 5.0\end{matrix} \left]\right.$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>The intersection point is inside the triangle because the barycentric weights for $$\textbf{x}(5)$$ are all positive.</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Definition
snippet: Definition: Definition A convex combination of points \textbf{v}_{1},\textbf{v}_{2},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{k} in \mathbb{R}^{n} is a linear combination of the form c_{1} \textbf{v}_{1} + c_{2} \textbf{v}_{2} + \hdots + c_{k} \textbf{v}_{k}...
body_xml:
<note type="definition" source_type="definition" title="Definition">
    <heading level="2">Definition</heading>
    <paragraph>A convex combination of points $$\textbf{v}_{1},\textbf{v}_{2},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{k}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ is a linear combination of the form</paragraph>
    <paragraph>$$c_{1} \textbf{v}_{1} + c_{2} \textbf{v}_{2} + \hdots + c_{k} \textbf{v}_{k}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>such that $$c_{1} + c_{2} + \cdots + c_{k} = 1$$ and $$c_{i} \geq 0$$ for all $$i$$ . The set of all convex combinations of points in a set $$S$$ is called the convex hull of $$S$$ , denoted by $$\text{conv} S$$ .﻿</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Example 1
snippet: Example 1: Example 1 Let v_{1} = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}3 \\ 0 \\ 6 \\ - 3\end{matrix} \left]\right. , & & v_{2} = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}- 6 \\ 3 \\ 3 \\ 0\end{matrix} \left]\right. , & & v_{3} = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}3 \\...
body_xml:
<example number="1">
    <heading level="2">Example 1</heading>
    <paragraph>Let</paragraph>
    <paragraph>$$v_{1} = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}3 \\ 0 \\ 6 \\ - 3\end{matrix} \left]\right. , & & v_{2} = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}- 6 \\ 3 \\ 3 \\ 0\end{matrix} \left]\right. , & & v_{3} = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}3 \\ 6 \\ 0 \\ 3\end{matrix} \left]\right. , & & p_{1} = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}0 \\ 3 \\ 3 \\ 0\end{matrix} \left]\right. , & & p_{2} = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}- 10 \\ 5 \\ 11 \\ - 4\end{matrix} \left]\right. ,$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>and $$S = \left\{ \textbf{v}_{1},\textbf{v}_{2},\textbf{v}_{3} \right\}$$ . Note that $$S$$ is an orthogonal set. Determine whether $$\textbf{p}_{1}$$ is in $$\text{Span} S$$ , $$\text{aff} S$$ , and $$\text{conv} S$$ . Then do the same for $$\textbf{p}_{2}$$ .﻿</paragraph>
    <heading level="3">Solution</heading>
    <paragraph>If $$\textbf{p}_{1}$$ is at least a linear combination of the points in $$S$$ , then the weights are easily found, because $$S$$ is an orthogonal set. Let $$W$$ be the subspace spanned by $$S$$ . A calculation as in Section 6.3 shows that the orthogonal projection of $$\textbf{p}_{1}$$ onto $$W$$ is $$\textbf{p}_{1}$$ itself:</paragraph>
    <paragraph>$$\text{proj} _{W } \mathbf{p}_{1} & = & \frac{\mathbf{p}_{1} \cdot \mathbf{v}_{1}}{\mathbf{v}_{1} \cdot \mathbf{v}_{1}} \mathbf{v}_{1} + \frac{\mathbf{p}_{1} \cdot \mathbf{v}_{2}}{\mathbf{v}_{2} \cdot \mathbf{v}_{2}} \mathbf{v}_{2} + \frac{\mathbf{p}_{1} \cdot \mathbf{v}_{3}}{\mathbf{v}_{3} \cdot \mathbf{v}_{3}} \mathbf{v}_{3} & = & \frac{18}{54} \mathbf{v}_{1} + \frac{18}{54} \mathbf{v}_{2} + \frac{18}{54} \mathbf{v}_{3} & = & \frac{1}{3} \left[\right. \begin{matrix}3 \\ 0 \\ 6 \\ - 3\end{matrix} \left]\right. + \frac{1}{3} \left[\right. \begin{matrix}- 6 \\ 3 \\ 3 \\ 0\end{matrix} \left]\right. + \frac{1}{3} \left[\right. \begin{matrix}3 \\ 6 \\ 0 \\ 3\end{matrix} \left]\right. = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}0 \\ 3 \\ 3 \\ 0\end{matrix} \left]\right. = \mathbf{p}_{1}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>This shows that $$\textbf{p}_{1}$$ is in $$\text{Span} S$$ . Also, since the coefficients sum to $$1$$ , $$\textbf{p}_{1}$$ is in $$\text{aff} S$$ . In fact, $$\textbf{p}_{1}$$ is in $$\text{conv} S,$$ because the coefficients are also nonnegative.</paragraph>
    <paragraph>For $$\mathbf{p}_{2}$$ , a similar calculation shows that $$\text{proj} _{W}\mathbf{p}_{2} \neq \mathbf{p}_{2}$$ . Since $$\text{proj} _{W}\mathbf{p}_{2}$$ is the closest point in $$\text{Span} S$$ to $$\mathbf{p}_{2}$$ , the point $$\mathbf{p}_{2}$$ is not in $$\text{Span} S$$ . In particular, $$\mathbf{p}_{2}$$ cannot be in $$\text{aff} S$$ or $$\text{conv} S$$ .﻿</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Example 3
snippet: Example 3: Example 3 Let S = \left\{ {\begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix}:x \geq 0{and}y = x^{2}} \right\} . Show that the convex hull of S is the union of the origin and \left\{ {\begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix}:x > 0{and}y \geq...
body_xml: Example 3 Let $$S = \left\{ {\begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix}:x \geq 0{and}y = x^{2}} \right\}$$ . Show that the convex hull of $$S$$ is the union of the origin and $$\left\{ {\begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix}:x > 0{and}y \geq x^{2}} \right\}$$ . See Figure 3. Solution Every point in $$\text{conv} S$$ must lie on a line segment that connects two points of $$S$$ . The dashed line in Figure 3 indicates that, except for the origin, the positive $$y \text{-axis}$$ is not in $$\text{conv} S$$ , because the origin is the only point of $$S$$ on the $$y \text{-axis}$$ . It may seem reasonable that Figure 3 does show $$\text{conv} S,$$ but how can you be sure that the point $$(10^{- 2},10^{4})$$ , for example, is on a line segment from the origin to a point on the curve in $$S$$ ? Consider any point $$\textbf{p}$$ in the shaded region of Figure 3, say $$\mathbf{p} = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}a \\ b\end{matrix} \left]\right. , & \text{with} a > 0 \text{and} b \geq a^{2}$$ The line through $$\textbf{0}$$ and $$\textbf{p}$$ has the equation $$y = (b/a)t$$ for $$t$$ real. That line intersects $$S$$ where $$t$$ satisfies $$(b/a)t = t^{2},$$ that is, when $$t = b/a.$$ Thus, $$\textbf{p}$$ is on the line segment from $$0$$ to $$\begin{bmatrix} {b/a} \\ {b^{2}/a^{2}} \end{bmatrix}$$ , which shows that Figure 3 is correct.

<example number="4">
    <heading level="2">Example 4</heading>
    <paragraph>Let</paragraph>
    <paragraph>$$\mathbf{v}_{1} = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}1 \\ 0\end{matrix} \left]\right. , & & \mathbf{v}_{2} = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}2 \\ 3\end{matrix} \left]\right. , & & \mathbf{v}_{3} = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}5 \\ 4\end{matrix} \left]\right. , & & \mathbf{v}_{4} = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}3 \\ 0\end{matrix} \left]\right. , & & \mathbf{p} = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}\frac{10}{3} \\ \frac{5}{2}\end{matrix} \left]\right. ,$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>and $$S = \left\{ \textbf{v}_{1},\textbf{v}_{2},\textbf{v}_{3},\textbf{v}_{4} \right\}$$ . Then</paragraph>
    <paragraph>(2)</paragraph>
    <paragraph>$$\frac{1}{4} \textbf{v}_{1} + \frac{1}{6} \textbf{v}_{2} + \frac{1}{2} \textbf{v}_{3} + \frac{1}{12} \textbf{v}_{4} = \textbf{p}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Use the procedure in the proof of Caratheodory’s Theorem to express $$\textbf{p}$$ as a convex combination of three points of $$S$$ .﻿</paragraph>
    <heading level="3">Solution</heading>
    <paragraph>The set $$S$$ is affinely dependent. Use the technique of Section 8.2 to obtain an affine dependence relation</paragraph>
    <paragraph>(3)</paragraph>
    <paragraph>$$- 5 \textbf{v}_{1} + 4 \textbf{v}_{2} - 3 \textbf{v}_{3} + 4 \textbf{v}_{4} = \textbf{0}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Next, choose the points $$\textbf{v}_{2}$$ and $$\textbf{v}_{4}$$ in (3), whose coefficients are positive. For each point, compute the ratio of the coefficients in equations (2) and (3). The ratio for $$\textbf{v}_{2}$$ is $$\frac{1}{6} \div 4 = \frac{1}{24}$$ , and that for $$\textbf{v}_{4}$$ is $$\frac{1}{12} \div 4 = \frac{1}{48}$$ . The ratio for $$\textbf{v}_{4}$$ is smaller, so subtract $$\frac{1}{48}$$ times equation (3) from equation (2) to eliminate $$\textbf{v}_{4}$$ :</paragraph>
    <paragraph>$$\left(\frac{1}{4} + \frac{5}{48}\right) \textbf{v}_{1} + \left(\frac{1}{6} - \frac{4}{48}\right) \textbf{v}_{2} + \left(\frac{1}{2} + \frac{3}{48}\right) \textbf{v}_{3} + \left(\frac{1}{12} - \frac{4}{48}\right) \textbf{v}_{4} = \textbf{p} \frac{17}{48} \textbf{v}_{1} + \frac{4}{48} \textbf{v}_{2} + \frac{27}{48} \textbf{v}_{3} = \textbf{p}$$</paragraph>
  </example>

<note type="definition" source_type="definition" title="Definition">
    <heading level="2">Definition</heading>
    <paragraph>A linear functional on $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ is a linear transformation $$f$$ from $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ into $$\mathbb{R}$$ . For each scalar $$d$$ in $$\mathbb{R}$$ , the symbol $$[\textit{f} \text{:} d]$$ denotes the set of all $$\textbf{x}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ at which the value of $$f$$ is $$d$$ . That is,</paragraph>
    <paragraph>$$[ \textit{f} : d ] & \text{is} \text{the} \text{set} & \left{\right. \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^{n} : f \left(\right. \mathbf{x} \left.\right) = d \left.\right}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>The zero functional is the transformation such that $$f(\textbf{x}) = 0$$ for all $$\textbf{x}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ . All other linear functionals on $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ are said to be nonzero.</paragraph>
  </note>

  </example>

title: Example 5
snippet: Example 5: Example 5 Let \textbf{v}_{1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} and \textbf{v}_{2} = \begin{bmatrix} 6 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} , and let L_{1} be the line through \textbf{v}_{1} and \textbf{v}_{2} . Find a linear functional f and...
body_xml:
<example number="5">
    <heading level="2">Example 5</heading>
    <paragraph>Let $$\textbf{v}_{1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}$$ and $$\textbf{v}_{2} = \begin{bmatrix} 6 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}$$ , and let $$L_{1}$$ be the line through $$\textbf{v}_{1}$$ and $$\textbf{v}_{2}$$ . Find a linear functional $$f$$ and a constant $$d$$ such that $$L_{1} = {[f \text{:} d]}$$ .﻿</paragraph>
    <heading level="3">Solution</heading>
    <paragraph>The line $$L_{1}$$ is parallel to the translated line $$L_{0}$$ through $$\textbf{v}_{2} - \textbf{v}_{1}$$ and the origin. The defining equation for $$L_{0}$$ has the form</paragraph>
    <paragraph>(5)</paragraph>
    <paragraph>$$\left[\right. \begin{matrix}a & b\end{matrix} \left]\right. \left[\right. \begin{matrix}x \\ y\end{matrix} \left]\right. = 0 & \text{or} & n \cdot x = 0 , & \text{where} & n = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}a \\ b\end{matrix} \left]\right.$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Since $$\textbf{n}$$ is orthogonal to the subspace $$L_{0}$$ , which contains $$\textbf{v}_{2} - \textbf{v}_{1}$$ , compute</paragraph>
    <paragraph>$$\textbf{v}_{2} - \textbf{v}_{1} = \begin{bmatrix} 6 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} - \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ - 2 \end{bmatrix}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>and solve</paragraph>
    <paragraph>$$\begin{bmatrix} a & b \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ - 2 \end{bmatrix} = 0$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>By inspection, a solution is $${[\begin{matrix} a & b \end{matrix}]} = {[\begin{matrix} 2 & 5 \end{matrix}]}$$ . Let $$f(x,y) = 2x + 5y$$ . From (5), $$L_{0} = \lbrack f:0\rbrack$$ , and $$L_{1} = \lbrack f:d\rbrack$$ for some $$d$$ . Since $$\textbf{v}_{1}$$ is on line $$L_{1}$$ , $$d = f\left( \textbf{v}_{1} \right) = 2(1) + 5(2) = 12$$ . Thus, the equation for $$L_{1}$$ is $$2x + 5y = 12$$ . As a check, note that $$f\left( \textbf{v}_{2} \right) = f(6,0) = 2(6) + 5(0) = 12$$ , so $$\textbf{v}_{2}$$ is on $$L_{1}$$ , too.</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Example 6
snippet: Example 6: Example 6 Let \textbf{v}_{1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} , \textbf{v}_{2} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ {- 1} \\ 4 \end{bmatrix} , and \textbf{v}_{3} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} . Find an implicit...
body_xml:
<example number="6">
    <heading level="2">Example 6</heading>
    <paragraph>Let $$\textbf{v}_{1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$$ , $$\textbf{v}_{2} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ {- 1} \\ 4 \end{bmatrix}$$ , and $$\textbf{v}_{3} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}$$ . Find an implicit description $$\left\lbrack {{f} \text{:} d} \right\rbrack$$ of the plane $$H_{1}$$ that passes through $$\textbf{v}_{1}$$ , $$\textbf{v}_{2}$$ , and $$\textbf{v}_{3}$$ .﻿</paragraph>
    <heading level="3">Solution</heading>
    <paragraph>$$H_{1}$$ is parallel to a plane $$H_{0}$$ through the origin that contains the translated points</paragraph>
    <paragraph>$$v_{2} - v_{1} = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}1 \\ - 2 \\ 3\end{matrix} \left]\right. & \text{and} & v_{3} - v_{1} = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{matrix} \left]\right.$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Since these two points are linearly independent, $$H_{0} = \text{Span} \left\{ \textbf{v}_{2} - \textbf{v}_{1},\textbf{v}_{3} - \textbf{v}_{1} \right\}$$ . Let $$\textbf{n} = \begin{bmatrix} a \\ b \\ c \end{bmatrix}$$ be the normal to $$H_{0}$$ . Then $$\textbf{v}_{2} - \textbf{v}_{1}$$ and $$\textbf{v}_{3} - \textbf{v}_{1}$$ are each orthogonal to $$\textbf{n}$$ . That is, $$(\textbf{v}_{2} - \textbf{v}_{1}) \cdot \textbf{n} = 0$$ and $$\left( \textbf{v}_{3} - \textbf{v}_{1} \right) \cdot \textbf{n} = 0$$ . These two equations form a system whose augmented matrix can be row reduced:</paragraph>
    <paragraph>$$\left[\right. \begin{matrix}1 & - 2 & 3\end{matrix} \left]\right. \left[\right. \begin{matrix}a \\ b \\ c\end{matrix} \left]\right. = 0 , & \left[\right. \begin{matrix}2 & 0 & 1\end{matrix} \left]\right. \left[\right. \begin{matrix}a \\ b \\ c\end{matrix} \left]\right. = 0 , & \left[\right. \begin{matrix}1 & - 2 & 3 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 1 & 0\end{matrix} \left]\right.$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Row operations yield $$a = \left( - \frac{2}{4} \right)c$$ , $$b = \left( \frac{5}{4} \right)c$$ , with $$c$$ free. Set $$c = 4$$ , for instance. Then $$\textbf{n} = \begin{bmatrix} {- 2} \\ 5 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix}$$ and $$H_{0} = [\textit{f} \text{:0]}$$ , where $$f\left( \textbf{x} \right) = - 2x_{1} + 5x_{2} + 4x_{3}$$ .﻿</paragraph>
    <paragraph>The parallel hyperplane $$H_{1}$$ is $$\lbrack f:d\rbrack$$ . To find $$d$$ , use the fact that $$\textbf{v}_{1}$$ is in $$H_{1}$$ , and compute $$d = f\left( \textbf{v}_{1} \right) = f(1,1,1) = - 2(1) + 5(1) + 4(1) = 7$$ . As a check, compute $$f\left( \textbf{v}_{2} \right) = f(2, - 1,4) = - 2(2) + 5( - 1) + 4(4) = 16 - 9 = 7$$ . Observe $$f(\textbf{v}_{3}) = 7$$ also.</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Theorem ﻿11﻿
snippet: Theorem ﻿11﻿: Theorem ﻿11﻿ A subset H of \mathbb{R}^{n} is a hyperplane if and only if H = \lbrack f:d\rbrack for some nonzero linear functional f and some scalar d in \mathbb{R} . Thus, if H is a hyperplane, there exist a nonzero vector...

<note type="procedure" source_type="procedure" title="Theorem ﻿11﻿">
    <heading level="2">Theorem ﻿11﻿</heading>
    <paragraph>A subset $$H$$ of $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ is a hyperplane if and only if $$H = \lbrack f:d\rbrack$$ for some nonzero linear functional $$f$$ and some scalar $$d$$ in $$\mathbb{R}$$ . Thus, if $$H$$ is a hyperplane, there exist a nonzero vector $$\textbf{n}$$ and a real number $$d$$ such that $$H = \left\{ \textbf{x}:\textbf{n} \cdot \textbf{x} = d \right\}$$ .﻿</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Topology in ℝn﻿: Terms and Facts
snippet: Topology in ℝn﻿: Terms and Facts: Topology in ℝn﻿: Terms and Facts For any point \textbf{p} in \mathbb{R}^{n} and any real \delta > 0 , the open ball B(\textbf{p},\delta) with center \textbf{p} and radius \delta is given by B \left(\right....
body_xml:
<note type="procedure" source_type="procedure_box" title="Topology in ℝn﻿: Terms and Facts">
    <heading level="2">Topology in ℝn﻿: Terms and Facts</heading>
    <paragraph>For any point $$\textbf{p}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ and any real $$\delta > 0$$ , the open ball $$B(\textbf{p},\delta)$$ with center $$\textbf{p}$$ and radius $$\delta$$ is given by</paragraph>
    <paragraph>$$B \left(\right. \textbf{p} , \delta \left.\right) = \left{\right. \textbf{x} : \parallel \textbf{x} - \textbf{p} \parallel < \delta \left.\right}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Given a set $$S$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ , a point $$\textbf{p}$$ is an interior point of $$S$$ if there exists a $$\delta > 0$$ such that $$B\left( \textbf{p},\delta \right) \subseteq S$$ . If every open ball centered at $$\textbf{p}$$ intersects both $$S$$ and the complement of $$S$$ , then $$\textbf{p}$$ is called a boundary point of $$S$$ . A set is open if it contains none of its boundary points. (This is equivalent to saying that all of its points are interior points.) A set is closed if it contains all of its boundary points. (If $$S$$ contains some but not all of its boundary points, then $$S$$ is neither open nor closed.) A set $$S$$ is bounded if there exists a $$\delta > 0$$ such that $$S \subseteq B\left( \textbf{0},\delta \right)$$ . A set in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ is compact if it is closed and bounded.</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Theorem: The convex hull of an open set is open, and the convex hull of a compact set is compact. (The convex hull of a closed set need not be closed. See Exercise 33.)</paragraph>
  </note>

Then $$\textbf{p}_{1}$$ is an interior point since $$B\left( {\textbf{p}_{1},\frac{3}{4}} \right) \subseteq S$$ . The point $$\textbf{p}_{2}$$ is a boundary point since every open ball centered at $$\textbf{p}_{2}$$ intersects both $$S$$ and the complement of $$S$$ . The set $$S$$ is closed since it contains all its boundary points. The set $$S$$ is bounded since $$S \subseteq B\left( \textbf{0},3 \right)$$ . Thus $$S$$ is also compact.

title: ﻿Definition
snippet: ﻿Definition: ﻿Definition The hyperplane H = \left[\right. f : d \left]\right. separates two sets A and B if one of the following holds: f(A) \leq d and f(B) \geq d , or f(A) \geq d and f(B) \leq d .﻿ If in the conditions above all the weak...
body_xml:
<note type="definition" source_type="definition" title="﻿Definition">
    <heading level="2">﻿Definition</heading>
    <paragraph>The hyperplane $$H = \left[\right. f : d \left]\right.$$ separates two sets $$A$$ and $$B$$ if one of the following holds:</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>$$f(A) \leq d$$ and $$f(B) \geq d$$ , or</item>
      <item>$$f(A) \geq d$$ and $$f(B) \leq d$$ .﻿</item>
    </list>
    <paragraph>If in the conditions above all the weak inequalities are replaced by strict inequalities, then $$H$$ is said to strictly separate $$A$$ and $$B$$ .﻿</paragraph>
  </note>

snippet: ﻿﻿Theorem ﻿12﻿: ﻿﻿Theorem ﻿12﻿ Suppose A and B are nonempty convex sets such that A is compact and B is closed. Then there exists a hyperplane H that strictly separates A and B if and only if A \cap B = \varnothing .﻿

<note type="procedure" source_type="procedure" title="﻿﻿Theorem ﻿12﻿">

    <paragraph>Suppose $$A$$ and $$B$$ are nonempty convex sets such that $$A$$ is compact and $$B$$ is closed. Then there exists a hyperplane $$H$$ that strictly separates $$A$$ and $$B$$ if and only if $$A \cap B = \varnothing$$ .﻿</paragraph>

title: Example 8
snippet: Example 8: Example 8 Let \textbf{a}_{1} = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{matrix} \left]\right. , & \textbf{a}_{2} = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}- 3 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{matrix} \left]\right. , & \textbf{a}_{3} = \left[\right....
body_xml:
<example number="8">
    <heading level="2">Example 8</heading>
    <paragraph>Let</paragraph>
    <paragraph>$$\textbf{a}_{1} = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{matrix} \left]\right. , & \textbf{a}_{2} = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}- 3 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{matrix} \left]\right. , & \textbf{a}_{3} = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}3 \\ 4 \\ 0\end{matrix} \left]\right. , & \textbf{b}_{1} = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{matrix} \left]\right. , & \text{and} & \textbf{b}_{2} = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}2 \\ - 1 \\ 5\end{matrix} \left]\right. ,$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>and let $$A = \{\textbf{a}_{1},\textbf{a}_{2},\textbf{a}_{3}\}$$ and $$B = \left\{ \textbf{b}_{1},\textbf{b}_{2} \right\}$$ . Show that the hyperplane $$H = \lbrack f:5\rbrack$$ , where $$f\left( x_{1},x_{2},x_{3} \right) = 2x_{1} - 3x_{2} + x_{3}$$ , does not separate $$A$$ and $$B$$ . Is there a hyperplane parallel to $$H$$ that does separate $$A$$ and $$B$$ ? Do the convex hulls of $$A$$ and $$B$$ intersect?</paragraph>
    <heading level="3">Solution</heading>
    <paragraph>Evaluate the linear functional $$f$$ at each of the points in $$A$$ and $$B$$ :</paragraph>
    <paragraph>$$f \left(\right. a_{1} \left.\right) = 2 , & f \left(\right. a_{2} \left.\right) = - 11 , & f \left(\right. a_{3} \left.\right) = - 6 , & f \left(\right. b_{1} \left.\right) = 4 , & \text{and} & f \left(\right. b_{2} \left.\right) = 12$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Since $$f(\textbf{b}_{1}) = 4$$ is less than $$5$$ and $$f(\textbf{b}_{2}) = 12$$ is greater than $$5$$ , points of $$B$$ lie on both sides of $$H = \lbrack f:5\rbrack$$ and so $$H$$ does not separate $$A$$ and $$B$$ .﻿</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Since $$f(A) < 3$$ and $$f(B) > 3$$ , the parallel hyperplane $$\lbrack f:3\rbrack$$ strictly separates $$A$$ and $$B$$ . By Theorem 13, $$\text{(conv} A) \cap \text{(conv} B) = \varnothing$$ .﻿</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Caution: If there were no hyperplane parallel to $$H$$ that strictly separated $$A$$ and $$B$$ , this would not necessarily imply that their convex hulls intersect. It might be that some other hyperplane not parallel to $$H$$ would strictly separate them.</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Definition
snippet: Definition: Definition Let S be a compact convex subset of \mathbb{R}^{n} . A nonempty subset F of S is called a (proper) face of S if F \neq S and there exists a hyperplane H = \lbrack f:d\rbrack such that F = S \cap H and either f(S)...
body_xml:
<note type="definition" source_type="definition" title="Definition">
    <heading level="2">Definition</heading>
    <paragraph>Let $$S$$ be a compact convex subset of $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ . A nonempty subset $$F$$ of $$S$$ is called a (proper) face of $$S$$ if $$F \neq S$$ and there exists a hyperplane $$H = \lbrack f:d\rbrack$$ such that $$F = S \cap H$$ and either $$f(S) \leq d$$ or $$f(S) \geq d.$$ The hyperplane $$H$$ is called a supporting hyperplane to $$S$$ . If the dimension of $$F$$ is $$k$$ , then $$F$$ is called a $$\textit{\textbf{k}}\textbf{-face}$$ of $$S$$ .﻿</paragraph>
    <paragraph>If $$P$$ is a polytope of dimension $$k$$ , then $$P$$ is called a $$\mathbf{\mathit{k}}$$ -polytope. A $$\text{0-face}$$ of $$P$$ is called a vertex (plural: vertices), a $$\text{1-face}$$ is an edge, and a $$(k - 1)$$ -dimensional face is a facet of $$S$$ .﻿</paragraph>
  </note>

(See Figure 1.) $$H \cap S \text{may} \text{be} \text{a} \text{2} - \text{dimensional} \text{square} \text{face} ( \text{facet} ) \text{of} \text{the} \text{cube} . H \cap S \text{may} \text{be} \text{a} \text{1} - \text{dimensional} \text{edge} \text{of} \text{the} \text{cube} . H \cap S \text{may} \text{be} \text{a} \text{0} - \text{dimensional} \text{vertex} \text{of} \text{the} \text{cube} .$$

More precisely, if $$\textbf{x}$$ , $$\textbf{y} \in S$$ and $$\textbf{p} \in \overset{‾}{\textbf{xy}}$$ , then $$\textbf{p} = \textbf{x}$$ or $$\textbf{p} = \textbf{y}$$ .   </note>

body_xml: Example 2 Recall that the profile of a set $$S$$ is the set of extreme points of $$S$$ . Theorem 14 shows that the profile of a polygon in $$\mathbb{R}^{2}$$ is the set of vertices.
